title: Subscribe to Ars Technica - Ars Technica
text:
Gift an Ars Sub
Gifting a sub is easy, and it's the best way to share the love of Ars Technica! Enter your information and the
recipient's details, and we'll take care of the rest.
Give Ars Pro
Give Ars Pro++
An overview of what features come with your sub:
Ad-free experience
Ars subscribers get no banner ads, no video pre-rolls, and can enjoy Ars entirely ad-free while supporting our work
No trackers
Pages are completely tracker-free, offering an additional layer of privacy when you browse Ars
Ars Classic view
Browse the front page in the original blog-style format, with the first three paragraphs of each story visible
Neutron Star view
Super dense headline mode with keyboard navigation
Topic filtering
Subscribers can turn off topics they don’t want to see, and change the Most Read topic
Optimized reading layout
The ad-free experience includes a page layout that optimizes for content
Optional wide text mode
In addition to changing the text size and link colors subscribers can opt for a wider text column for increased page density
Full-text RSS feeds
Read all Ars content from your favorite RSS reader
Access to subscriber forums
Enjoy discussions with your fellow geeks in the Lounge, our safe haven from trolls and social media
PDF downloads
A convenient way to archive stories
Help Ars focus on its core journalistic mission
Your subscription helps Ars focus on its core journalistic mission
Frequently asked questions. Need another answer? Reach out to us!
I can already ad block, why pay for a sub?
Fair question. We hear you on not liking ads or trackers, it’s why our subscription doesn’t have either. Look around the industry, almost no one promises that. The truth is when you block ads you deprive us of support for our journalism.
Our subscription is not only ad-free, it offers a better reading experience than ad blocking, with clean page layouts, and features like extra-wide text mode, or Classic and Neutron Star home page views.
It also supports us directly, so you can help keep our journalism alive.
Why do you require a credit card for the free trial?
The main reason is it’s an easy way to keep people from abusing it by constantly signing up for free. But of course we hope you like it, want to keep it, and will smoothly transition into the full Ars Pro experience.
We have no desire to trick anyone. Canceling is easy if you don’t end up liking it.
Can I cancel my sub once I’ve paid for it?
You can always cancel your sub, and it will not automatically renew after expiration. We do not offer refunds under most circumstances, and your subscription benefits will continue to work until expiration, unless you ask for your account to be deleted.
Do you store my credit card info?
Ars Technica does not store or directly handle your credit card information. We use the leading subscription service provider Chargebee, in conjunction with either Stripe or PayPal. Your card number will be stored with one of those two providers, which in turn share a token with Chargebee that allows for recurring payments.
We will never see your card number, and we will never store it on our servers.
Can I upgrade or downgrade my subscription?
Yes! You can upgrade or downgrade your subscription at any time. If you upgrade, you will be charged the difference in price for the remaining time on your current subscription. If you downgrade, you will be charged the new rate at the end of your current billing cycle.
Can I gift a subscription?
Yes! You can gift a subscription to someone else. Just select one of the gifts from the subscribe page, and enter the recipient's email address. They will receive an email with your gift message and instructions on how to activate their subscription.
Can I use my subscription on multiple devices?
Yes! Your subscription is tied to your Ars Technica account, so you can use it on any device where you're logged in. This includes your computer, tablet, and smartphone.
What if I have more questions?
If you have any other questions, please feel free to reach out to us at our support email or use the form on our contact page. We're happy to help!

title: Updated Google privacy policy says your Gmail might be used for advertising - Ars Technica
text:
Using Google’s products and services has always been fundamentally precarious—doing so gives the world’s largest advertising company a lot of juicy personal data. Google has long said it won’t use the sensitive data from products like Gmail, Drive, and Photos for ad personalization, but a change to the company’s privacy policy appears to dismantle that firewall.
On October 16, Google issued an update to its privacy policy, spotted by Android Authority. The ad personalization section used to include a clear limit on data from certain apps. “We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos,” the document said. Now, Google has updated it with the following language.
Updated language on when your sensitive data might inform ads.
Credit:
Google
Updated language on when your sensitive data might inform ads.
Credit:
Google
This equivocation opens the door to using data from apps like Gmail and Photos in ads when it’s shared with other Google services, and it just so happens Google has a mechanism for doing that, with Personal Intelligence. The company released Personal Intelligence in early 2026, allowing users to hand data from multiple apps to Google AI products. The idea is that the added context from your existing data will lead to better AI answers, but it’s also proving to be a privacy minefield.
Personal Intelligence connects your data to the Gemini app but also to features like AI Mode search. While the Gemini app does not currently have ads, you may see sponsored content in AI search tools. Google’s changes to the privacy policy appear to acknowledge that data shared with AI search via Personal Intelligence could, therefore, contribute to ad personalization.
According to Google, this clarification still doesn’t mean ads are “based directly” on your personal data. Here’s the company’s full statement:
“Connecting your apps is entirely opt-in. Ads will continue to be relevant to things like your query, the context of the response and your interests. Ads will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or Photos library, and as always, sensitive information will not be used to tailor ads.”
Google’s statement is essentially a roundabout way of confirming that Workspace and Photos data may inform ads. If you interact with AI Mode while Personal Intelligence is enabled, there’s a chance that summaries and insights from your data will inform the answers you get. Because that same data is used for ad targeting, it’s accurate to say that your personal data is an element of ad targeting in AI search. The privacy policy now makes that clear.
A Google spokesperson tells Ars that its privacy clarification does not indicate a change in how it handles your data with respect to its advertising partners. It’s not scanning your entire inbox to enhance your advertising profile, and it’s not giving any of this data to third parties. But if you pipe personal data into an AI search tool, the ads it shows you could be based on that information.
The personalization trap
The core of the problem is that Google wants its products and services to talk to each other. Google sees that wealth of data as a key strength of its AI efforts. Some apps like Gmail are still given protected status in Google’s data handling, but there are now more avenues for that data to get out. The more data you share across Google’s ecosystem, the greater the risk to your privacy.
We’ve seen a similar exception in the way Google uses your AI interactions for model training. While Google says it doesn’t use personal data for AI training, it does use your inputs and the model outputs for that purpose. With Gemini integrated with so many services and connected to them via Personal Intelligence, those outputs may very well contain elements of your personal information. Google has said it tries to filter that content from the user activity controls, therefore keeping it out of training sets. However, it doesn’t promise it will always be successful.
Google is correct that Personal Intelligence is opt-in, but the company uses various prompts and pop-ups to entice users to turn it on without fully explaining the consequences. You may have turned it on without realizing.
If you want to ensure ads never use your personal data in this way, you’ll need to make sure Personal Intelligence is turned off. The easiest way is to access the Gemini settings for Personal Intelligence and disable the connected apps. These settings are also a few levels deep in your main Google account settings under Data & privacy > Personalization settings > Manage Personalized Recommendations in Search Services > Connected Content Apps. From there, you can disable connections to Workspace and Google Photos.

title: Intel gets waiver after worries fuzzy US ban on foreign-made robots may hit fabs - Ars Technica
text:
US chip champion Intel was so confused by the US government ban on foreign-made robots that it requested and received a waiver “out of an abundance of caution.” The tech company wanted to make sure that it could continue using certain robotic vehicles in its US chip fabs.
The uncertainty surrounding the Federal Communications Commission ban on certain foreign-made robots was revealed in the agency’s decision to grant Intel’s waiver request. On October 22, the FCC published its order allowing Intel to continue using the foreign-made robots in US semiconductor manufacturing facilities for a period of one year.
The robots in question are automated guided vehicles operating on “tracks or predefined paths” while often requiring operator oversight, according to Intel’s website. They help to move materials and items around within warehouses and factory floors.
Such robotic vehicles are typically manufactured by Japanese companies like Murata Machinery and Daifuku Co., according to Bloomberg News. But the exact types of robotic vehicles used by Intel were only identified in a “confidential appendix” that accompanied its request.
The FCC’s ban mainly covers new models of mobile robots, like humanoid robots and robot vacuums, and still allows for the import of robots previously approved for sale in the United States. But the agency rules seem to restrict major modifications to “previously authorized devices.”
Intel’s waiver request stated that it was “unclear” whether its robotic vehicles even qualify as robots covered by the FCC ban but said it sought relief just in case. The tech company also received approval to “make certain hardware, software, and firmware changes” that would help ensure the continued operation and maintenance of the robotic vehicles.
The tech company described the robotic vehicles as being “critical to its domestic semiconductor manufacturing operations” and argued that the ability to maintain the robots was crucial to avoiding any disruptions to chip production. It also said there are no US-made alternatives that meet the company’s requirements.
The FCC approval came within a week of when Intel filed its waiver request on October 16. That is not too surprising given the importance of Intel to the Trump administration’s plans for reshoring chip manufacturing—not to mention that the US government took an $8.9 billion equity stake in the chip company.
Meanwhile, the US robotics industry at large is still grappling with the consequences of the FCC ban on foreign-made robots, given that China is the world’s leading supplier of robots and robotic components. Ars previously talked with one US robotics distributor that has pivoted from importing China’s humanoid robots to opening a US manufacturing facility for robots.
Some analysts have warned that the US government’s attempt to boost domestic production of robots via the restrictions on foreign-made robots could backfire for US industry. A report by the market intelligence firm International Data Corporation looks forward to 2030 and estimates that the FCC rule could reduce US revenue from deploying humanoid robots by 58 percent compared to pre-restriction expectations.

title: Hackers got a four-day head start on epic PHP2Shell vulnerability - Ars Technica
text:
Amazon has warned that vulnerabilities in a programming language that underpins much of the Internet, discovered using AI tools, are being “broadly exploited” as governments and companies rush to secure their systems.
The world’s largest cloud computing provider on Wednesday said it had identified an attempt by hackers to exploit the bug four days before the weakness was disclosed to the public.
Amazon added the flaws were “now being broadly exploited in the wild.”
The US National Security Agency and UK authorities earlier on Wednesday warned that the vulnerabilities had left websites around the world critically exposed to hacking, as some governments in Europe were reportedly taking sites offline while they patched the two security flaws.
The vast impact of the bugs, uncovered with the help of OpenAI and Google models after being undetected for more than a decade, highlights the ability of AI to upend cybersecurity.
The release of new models earlier this year from Anthropic and OpenAI with powerful cyber capabilities prompted warnings from politicians and financial regulators and led the US government to temporarily limit their rollout.
The NSA on Wednesday warned all organizations using the programming language known as PHP to immediately update their systems or take them offline.
The developers responsible for maintaining PHP released software updates to patch the vulnerabilities earlier on Wednesday.
“These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database,” the NSA said. “If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommended that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.”
Researchers at two US cybersecurity groups, Calif and Wiz, discovered the vulnerabilities. Alphabet-owned Wiz estimated that the compromised programming language powered about 70 percent of all websites in the world.
“Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory,” OpenAI said on Wednesday. “To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did.”
“It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with Internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits,” the AI lab added.
OpenAI worked with PHP, Calif, and Wiz to verify the vulnerabilities and develop the patches.
The White House said federal agencies were assessing the potential impacts of the bugs on government systems and critical infrastructure.
PHP’s wide presence on the Internet is largely because WordPress, the most widely used website-building platform, is written primarily in PHP and relies on it to function.
The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre said the vulnerabilities could potentially allow a hacker to take control of a website’s server without needing a password or other login credentials. “The NCSC is encouraging UK organizations to take immediate action,” it said.

title: The new human-crafted Apple Music brand matters in an AI world - Ars Technica
text:
Apple just revealed a new brand identity for Apple Music, with the expected turn to Liquid Glass. I’m not much of a fan of their new design language in general; this is where I admit that I’m still running MacOS Sequoia and have grumpy things to say about rounded corner radii and text legibility.
It’s just a trend, it will pass, and at some point I’ll probably cave and upgrade when it starts actually affecting my ability to get work done, or more importantly get security updates. Once I adjust, I’ll stop noticing it, and life will go on.
As such, I wouldn’t normally find an obvious rebrand like this notable, much less feel like I had much to say about it. But then I happened to catch Apple’s behind-the-scenes video in my YouTube recommendations, and I realized I did have thoughts.
It’s a short clip, respecting your time at just a little over a minute long if you want to watch for yourself.
Let’s get the obvious part out of the way: It’s pretty peak Apple. More than a little pretentious, with all the resources a $5 trillion market cap can bring to bear on every problem.
There’s a design agency (TBWA/Media Arts Lab), a pop hitmaker music producer (Fred again.. and yes, that’s how you spell it), a whole crewed set with cameras and lighting, and a mineral oil tank equipped with a transducer to effectively transmit audio signals into physical ripples.
They shot a ton of footage of the oil (chosen for its higher viscosity) interacting with the branding printed on transparent panels. Fast Company has a nice detailed breakdown of the technical aspects if you want to dig in more.
It’s a little eye-rolly with the narration, but honestly also lovely in the execution and care. And it made me realize how much I think we’re all going to value this kind of hands-on, human crafting in an era where anything can be generated out of a prompt.
Like many Ars readers, I have feelings about generative AI imagery. It’s feeling increasingly impossible to avoid in daily life. My new favorite term is “slop ghouls.”
One really unfortunate side effect of that persistence is a new natural tendency to be suspicious of everything you see. Was that picture you just saw hand-drawn, or did someone prompt it into existence with styles stolen from human artists?
I see us increasingly place genuine value on not just human-created craft, but seeing the process behind it that shows the hands at work. This Apple video was a neat bit of promotion, but it also provided the receipts. Real people did real things in the physical world to make the final images and videos.
Some stills from the video showing the process and people
Credit:
Apple
Some stills from the video showing the process and people
Credit:
Apple
The final effect is obviously cleaned up and post-processed. But when I look at it now, I don’t just see Liquid Glass; I see the humans and their time and energy and creativity. To me, at least, that matters. Showing your work, proving the time you put in—I appreciate it. I’m slightly less grumpy for it!
Generative AI is likely here to stay. There’s no stuffing the genie back in the bottle. I probably need to find some peace with that, though I reserve the right to still yell at clouds about it. In the meantime, I think we should do more to celebrate human involvement in things and not be shy about showing the process and behind-the-scenes work.

title: OpenAI's latest AI models are coming to Google Cloud and Antigravity - Ars Technica
text:
Google would certainly prefer that everyone used its Gemini models with Google Cloud services, but soon, you’ll have more options. OpenAI and Google have come to an arrangement that will see the former’s frontier models arrive in Google Cloud services. Perhaps more importantly, GPT models will soon appear in Antigravity, Google’s agent-powered coding tool.
For enterprise customers and AI enthusiasts, OpenAI’s latest model will appear in Google’s “Model Garden” in the coming weeks, adding to its 200-plus options. The garden already offers access to Google’s Gemini models, as well as an assortment of open models like Mistral, Llama, and Gemma. Anthropic’s Claude AI has also been available for some time. Google says it’s now the only large cloud provider offering access to all three leading closed LLMs.
While OpenAI notes that Microsoft continues to be its primary cloud partner, the full suite of current GPT 6 and 6.1 models—Astra, Sol, and Luna—will launch on Google Cloud. Astra will naturally cost the most to run, but Google’s system supports dynamically moving workloads between LLMs based on performance, latency, and efficiency.
OpenAI models will be available to run entirely on Google’s infrastructure, with transactions handled via the Google Cloud Marketplace. For businesses with established Google Cloud spending commitments, this will make it easy to begin using GPT models in place of whatever they were using before.
Google says all three OpenAI LLMs are rolling out now in private preview for select enterprise customers. Anyone interested in getting early access to the latest GPT AI in Google Cloud can submit a request, which will enable access through the API even if they’re using Codex CLI or Codex Desktop. The inference just runs on Google’s systems.
Bringing GPT models to Google Cloud could be a big deal for enterprise, but even individual users could see some benefit from the deal. Alongside the Cloud deployment, GPT models will appear in the Google Antigravity client. Until now, Antigravity has supported Google’s Gemini as well as Claude. Presumably, the same trio of OpenAI models will appear in Antigravity, but Google has not specified.
Google recently rolled out Gemini 4 Argon across its AI footprint, bringing its flagship AI back to parity with the competition—at least if you ask Google. It does seem like an improvement over Gemini 3.1 Pro, but it burns through tokens at an astonishing rate. Anthropic’s Claude models are already supported in Google Cloud, but the OpenAI deal will offer another alternative to Gemini for those not feeling the Argon love.

title: Judge rejects Trump’s wild claim EPA can dismiss data center pollution lawsuits - Ars Technica
text:
Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI is stuck facing a lawsuit over alleged data center pollution after Donald Trump failed to convince a judge that his Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has complete control over all Clean Air Act lawsuits and can dismiss any suit at whim.
Soon after unpermitted gas turbines were discovered powering Musk’s giant Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee, the NAACP sued. Its lawsuit sought an injunction requiring xAI (which, following a merger, is known now as SpaceXAI) to use the best available pollution control technology when operating the turbines and ordering penalties up to $124,426 per day per violation. Without such remedies, the turbines risked drastically spiking pollution in already vulnerable neighborhoods housing predominantly Black communities nearby, the NAACP argued.
To block the lawsuit, Trump tried to intervene, arguing that the EPA had the power to unilaterally dismiss lawsuits any time the president decides against enforcing the Clean Air Act. According to Trump, it would supposedly “not serve the public interest” if citizens were allowed to seek massive civil penalties to punish polluting AI firms that were trying to get data centers operational as fast as possible to support Trump’s AI Action Plan.
But Trump’s efforts to spare Musk’s firm were halted by a federal judge Tuesday, who ruled that “nothing” in the Clean Air Act (CAA) allows the EPA Administrator to “unilaterally dismiss a citizen suit.”
Such a power grab would seemingly give Trump authority to block any lawsuits alleging data center pollution, US District Judge Debra Brown’s order suggested. Even further, she observed that Trump could have used the authority to defend any interests against CAA lawsuits, not just the AI industry’s.
The NAACP had argued that the CAA’s text is focused “on ensuring air pollution standards are met and people are protected.” It urged the court to recognize that there is “no way to read” a provision granting citizens a right to sue as Trump has. That would “suggest that Congress, having gone out of its way to preserve people’s ability to sue to stop unlawful pollution when the government has not, also implicitly authorized the government to dismiss those very suits at its whim because it would prefer that the unlawful pollution continue,” the NAACP successfully argued.
In a press release, Laura Thoms—an enforcement director for an environmental group called Earthjustice that has partnered with the NAACP to support the lawsuit—accused Trump of seeking “unilateral and unreviewable veto power over citizen suits.”
“The Trump Administration has gone out of its way to shield Elon Musk’s company, [SpaceXAI], from liability and to deny local communities their right to protect themselves against illegal pollution,” Thoms said.
Thoms’ group is monitoring data center fights nationwide, not just SpaceXAI’s Colossus fight. However, Musk’s company’s battle was the first to expose the AI industry’s increasingly common practice of using unpermitted gas turbines to keep data center goals on target. So, Brown’s ruling is likely viewed as a big win for Americans worried Trump might make it impossible to stop the AI industry from polluting communities at a critical moment when data center demand for gas turbines is exploding.
Praising the court for “denying the US’s unprecedented and alarming argument,” Thoms vowed to “continue the fight to hold xAI accountable for the illegal air pollution it has been pumping out around the clock.”
Trump’s deeply flawed argument
Brown slammed the Trump EPA’s reading of the CAA as an “extraordinary position” with no grounding in federal law.
Trump tried to warp a single exception that lets the EPA dismiss a CAA lawsuit when it is either suing to require CAA enforcement or otherwise acting to require compliance.
Neither situation applies in this case, where the Trump administration has made it clear that it has no intention to sue SpaceXAI over the alleged violations. The federal government’s decision to ignore the problem is partly why the citizen lawsuit is necessary, the NAACP argued.
In that scenario where Trump could have dismissed the NAACP’s lawsuit, courts recognize that a citizen lawsuit could clash with government efforts to enforce the CAA or reach agreements with violators. But in the SpaceXAI lawsuit, Trump argued that the government’s right to intervene, which is sometimes used to dismiss lawsuits, was enough to shut down this lawsuit, regardless of the other facts.
Brown pointed out that it made no sense to argue that citizens can’t raise CAA lawsuits that the EPA opposes when the CAA also grants a right to sue the EPA administrator for failing to enforce the CAA.
“Evidently, Congress contemplated that citizen suits may not always align with the EPA’s judgment,” Brown wrote.
Congress even contemplated granting powers close to the authority Trump’s EPA tried to assert in this case, Brown said in a footnote. In 1990, Congress considered amending the CAA so that the EPA could substitute itself and take control of citizen suits over alleged violations. Had that happened, Trump may have been able to step in and drop the lawsuit. However, Congress did not adopt that amendment back in 1990, and Brown suggested that the mere consideration of the amendment favored the NAACP’s reading of the CAA.
“At most, the proposed amendment is evidence that at least some members of the 1990 Congress believed that the citizen suit provision as written does not allow the Administrator to intervene and subsequently terminate a citizen plaintiff’s claim,” Brown wrote.
Judge denies EPA veto power
Brown also acknowledged that the NAACP’s argument that every case Trump tried to use to seize power to veto the lawsuit “arose in a context where a government acted to require abatement of unlawful pollution, not one where the government acted to shield the polluter from liability.”
Ultimately, she agreed that “because the Administrator has not taken any action to enforce the Clean Air Act here, these cases do not support the United States’ position.”
Trump seemed particularly upset that SpaceXAI may face large fines. He argued that “punishing unlawful conduct through civil penalties payable to the Treasury on behalf of the United States is ‘a quintessentially executive power.’” As Trump explained, because the CAA is too vague on this point, “the canon of constitutional avoidance” applies, and courts must err on the side of his administration. Simply dismissing the lawsuit would avoid a constitutional clash, Trump argued.
But once again, Brown disagreed.
The US “fails to identify any ambiguity in the statute’s text to which the Court could and should apply the canon of constitutional avoidance,” Brown wrote. Rejecting Trump’s constitutional “doubts,” she concluded that “constitutional avoidance does not allow the Court to invent a right that does not exist in the statute.”
“That the Clean Air Act’s citizen suit provision allows private parties to enforce the Clean Air Act through civil litigation, therefore, does not make citizen suits an impermissible exercise of the President’s executive power,” Brown wrote. And “it does not follow that all suits seeking civil penalties require the exercise of nondelegable executive power.”
Had Trump succeeded, Americans who are increasingly opposing data centers nationwide may have been widely blocked from seeking fines when pollution can be proven.
Brown said the CAA cannot be interpreted that way, though, since “it can scarcely be doubted that, for a plaintiff who is injured or faces the threat of future injury due to illegal conduct ongoing at the time of suit, a sanction that effectively abates that conduct and prevents its recurrence provides a form of redress. Civil penalties can fit that description.” Critically, “to the extent that they encourage defendants to discontinue current violations and deter them from committing future ones, they afford redress to citizen plaintiffs who are injured or threatened with injury as a consequence of ongoing unlawful conduct,” Brown wrote.
Trump never explained intervention
When Trump took his first stab at blocking the lawsuit this summer, he didn’t cite EPA authority, just his own. He later amended his motion to specify that he was intervening on behalf of the EPA after the NAACP, and the court immediately pointed out fatal flaws in his arguments.
Since then, Brown’s order suggests that Trump’s efforts to kill Musk’s lawsuit stayed messy.
As a prime example, Trump goofed up by prematurely filing his appeal after the district court merely acknowledged at a hearing that it intended to dismiss the government’s motion to intervene to drop the suit. Without waiting for the actual opinion to drop, the US quickly went to an appeals court to reverse an order that did not exist yet, Brown said.
On the day that Brown at last issued her order, it did not say what Trump expected it to say. Parsing the actual order, the appeals court agreed that Trump had filed his appeal prematurely and denied Trump’s request to stay the district court’s litigation.
The appeals court denial came largely because Trump’s appeal was premised on Brown denying the government’s motion to intervene, which she did not. Although Brown denied Trump’s request to dismiss the lawsuit, she is still allowing the government to intervene on other grounds to support SpaceXAI, if that’s its intent.
That point remains somewhat unclear, as Brown noted that the government, in its rush to intervene, never said why it’s intervening—apart from bluntly demanding the suit be dropped. She gave the government until October 23 to either explain its position or stay out of the litigation.

title: The $15 billion ad-powered AI startup your doctor may already be using - Ars Technica
text:
Nearly two-thirds of US doctors are turning to an AI-powered search engine to make patient decisions, propelling a little-known tech startup to a $15 billion valuation while prompting a debate over the future of patient care.
Miami-based OpenEvidence, founded by serial entrepreneur Daniel Nadler in 2022, said that many of America’s 1 million physicians processed more than 42 million prompts last month. Doctors are using the company’s chatbot to scour medical journals and clinical guidelines to help diagnose and treat patients.
The ads-powered platform has grown largely by word of mouth, penetrating a sector where few tools have seen similar traction. “We’re the first viral consumer internet app in healthcare,” Nadler told the FT in an interview.
OpenEvidence has won praise from medical professionals who have found it helped ease workloads, according to interviews with eight senior physicians.
But it faces a nascent threat from large AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, who are making a push into the space. Its growing influence has also prompted scrutiny from researchers concerned over the accuracy of its results, as doctors grow more dependent on an AI tool shaping the course of treatments.
The company’s rapid ascent has attracted nearly $1 billion in investment in the past 18 months, from backers including Andreessen Horowitz, Blackstone, Thrive Capital, and Sequoia. The group raised $250 million in its latest funding round in September at a $15 billion valuation.
OpenEvidence booked $100 million in “ad buys”—a metric that covers current and future advertising commitments—for this year at the end of 2025, according to a person close to the company. The startup is on track to generate between $400 million and $500 million through ads by the end of 2026, the person added.
Credit:
OpenEvidence
Credit:
OpenEvidence
Nadler’s company has penetrated an established market for medical software that was sluggish to incorporate generative AI models. Dutch IT group Wolters Kluwer released an AI version of its leading subscription-based UpToDate medical software tool in October 2025, nearly two years after OpenEvidence entered the market.
Central to OpenEvidence’s pitch is a focused source list consisting of peer-reviewed journals such as the New England Journal of Medicine and the Journal of the American Medical Association.
“OpenEvidence allows me to provide a lot of context about my patient, find information, and make decisions faster,” said Nina Singh, a medical resident at the University of California San Francisco. “It’s a really useful tool.”
Widespread appeal has helped OpenEvidence forge relationships with several hospitals and specialist clinics such as Mount Sinai Health System and Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, embedding its tool within the organizations’ electronic health records.
Paul Testa, chief health informatics officer at NYU Langone, said that the hospital system sought a formal tie-up with OpenEvidence after it found clinicians were already using the tool as an “independent resource.”
“We chose to deeply integrate a clinically informed version of OpenEvidence into the care process to ensure two things: first, our clinicians can get the most from these AI tools, and second, they use them securely,” he said.
OpenEvidence has leveraged its popularity with doctors to slowly expand into other domains, including ambient documentation—note-taking during doctors’ patient interactions.
Critics have questioned whether the company’s ad-based model warrants its high valuation, while its decision to withdraw from the EU and UK earlier this year over the bloc’s AI Act has stymied its expansion into two key markets.
Mike Vernal, a partner at venture firm Conviction and an OpenEvidence investor, said that the company’s popularity among physicians represented its strongest defense against startup rivals and incumbents.
Nadler said it will also launch clinical trials in the coming weeks, partnering with researchers to target cancer and rare diseases. It plans to apply AI models to drug discovery and draw on pre-existing literature to generate novel scientific hypotheses.
“The end game is literature-based drug discovery,” Nadler said, referencing the field of data mining scientific literature for insights. “The economic value of that as a company is going to dwarf by orders of magnitude whatever we could have charged hospitals or advertisers.”
Alexander Tarashansky, the creator of Claude Science, an Anthropic platform that supports research scientists, has also joined the company to support its clinical work.
The company needs to see off competition from frontier AI companies such as OpenAI, which has also made a play for the space with ChatGPT for healthcare. Anthropic has also released healthcare tools, though it recently partnered with OpenEvidence to bring the tools to 100 low- and middle-income countries.
“The fact that doctors are adopting and using a piece of software of their own volition means there is a degree of differentiation that OpenEvidence can really lean on,” said Nworah Ayogu, a partner at investor Thrive Capital.
But analysis of OpenEvidence’s effectiveness has led to mixed results.
One study by the Mayo Clinic, an investor in the startup, found that it “provided accurate, evidence-based recommendations” in all five patient case studies that were sampled, although its impact on treatment decisions was more limited.
Other research, including a June paper published in Nature, found that it underperformed general-purpose AI models such as Google’s Gemini and OpenAI’s GPT on clinical benchmarks.
Eric Oermann, a neurosurgeon at NYU Langone, said there was a lack of research into the performance of individual AI tools and scant guidance on how to implement the tools in a clinical setting.
There are also widely held concerns that more junior doctors could fall foul by relying too heavily on OpenEvidence and other systems without first mastering basic knowledge of particular conditions and their prescribed treatment options.
“It’s a fun, friendly competitive pressure to play with benchmarks… [But] there’s no question of what AI tool physicians trust and use,” Nadler said.
Additional reporting by George Hammond in San Francisco.

title: Meta drops the word "train" from its commercial TOS after AI backlash - Ars Technica
text:
Hoping to quell criticism, Meta has dropped the word “train” from its “streamlined” commercial terms of service that kick in on October 30.
Last week, Meta faced backlash after legal experts warned that the tech giant’s sweeping new commercial terms of service seemed to give Meta permission to endlessly scrape websites linked on business pages. Talking to Nieman Lab, experts suggested that Meta could possibly use the policy to avoid millions in licensing fees from news organizations by requiring all business users to share a wealth of AI training data simply for running a business page.
A Meta spokesperson confirmed that Meta did not alert users to the changed language following backlash. This potentially only adds to confusion ahead of the policy rollout. In response to backlash, Meta’s spokesperson provided a statement to Ars, acknowledging Nieman Lab’s initial report but not its follow-up report reiterating experts’ concerns:
“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences. This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”
The same experts who sounded the initial alarms were not impressed by Meta’s updates, which they told Nieman Lab do not go far enough to protect business page users from invasive scraping. Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, told Nieman Lab that “publishers should remain concerned.”
“The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product,’” Topic said. “That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train.’”
What do updated terms say?
Initially, Meta’s terms authorized Meta to use “any content” from websites posted on business pages “to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity” of any Meta products, services, or features.
The updated terms delete the word “train” and no longer refer to “any content.” Instead, they allow Meta to “periodically pull updates” from business users’ websites in order to “provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products,” as well as to help Meta “maintain the integrity and security” of its products. This scraping, Meta says, is for users’ benefit, feeding into Meta research into products to “help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content, provide users information about your products and services, and connect you with users who may be interested in your products and services,” the policy says.
Following tweaks, it’s good that Meta added “more language about the permitted uses,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, told Nieman Lab. But “[the] ‘develop…advertising and business products’ [language] is still broad enough to drive a truck through,” he said. Ultimately, Grimmelmann agreed with Topic that “this does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites.”
What would help—as University of Wisconsin law professor Benjamin Sobel told Nieman Lab—would be if Meta added specific language to the policy where the company agrees to respect scraping instructions in robots.txt files. Since complying with robots.txt is voluntary, Meta could possibly rely on the legally enforceable TOS omitting mentions of robots.txt to scrape sites that attempt to block scraping via robots.txt, experts suggested.
When it comes to robots.txt, “you can still express the preference, and unless it’s a legally enforceable preference, it can still be ignored all the same,” Sobel said.
Meta backlash is global
Criticism goes beyond Nieman Lab’s reporting, as news groups globally urge regulators to intervene and block Meta’s controversial terms from kicking in.
A chief executive for the United Kingdom News Media Association, Theo Bamber, accused Meta of a “shameless land grab” relying on the “worst kind of arrogant tech platform bullying.” Bamber urged UK regulators to “stand up for British creators and the business community” by “preventing Meta from setting this dreadful precedent.”
Meanwhile, the European Publishers Council has already asked the European Commission to intervene. “Publishers must be able to decide whether and how their journalism is used, and negotiate fair payment,” the group’s executive director, Angela Mills Wad, said. “Burying such far-reaching claims in platform terms is no substitute for consent.”
Similarly, Danielle Coffey, the president and CEO of the News/Media Alliance—which Nieman Lab noted is the largest news publishing trade association in the US—protested the terms as “outrageous and probably illegal.”
In the US, Coffey urged regulators to recognize that Meta’s “decision to withhold access to its audience unless businesses allow Meta to scrape content from their websites is an appalling, bad-faith policy, and a clear abuse of the company’s market power.”
“It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30,” Coffey said.

Handheld gaming systems aren't niche anymore. Today's devices range from compact devices built around retro emulation to full-fledged portable PCs capable of running modern AAA games. That variety is exciting, but it also makes shopping harder. The "best" gaming handheld now depends less on a single, standout device and more on how, where and what you want to play.
Some handhelds are designed for quick sessions and classic libraries, prioritizing simplicity, long battery life and pocketable designs. Others blur the line between console and PC, offering large screens, powerful chips and access to massive game libraries, often at the cost of size, price or endurance. There are even more experimental options that focus on unusual controls or intentionally limited experiences.
We've spent months testing and tracking the fast-moving handheld space to figure out which devices are actually worth your money right now. Whether you're looking for a versatile all-rounder, a premium portable gaming PC or a dedicated machine for retro games, these are the gaming handhelds that stand out in an increasingly crowded field.
Editor's note (11/7/25): A barrage of new mobile emulation handhelds have been announced since our last update, including two follow-ups to our current "best for most" pick (the Retroid Pocket 6 and the more marginally updated Retroid Pocket G2) and a new version of our "best overall" pick (the AYN Odin 3). Other competitors like Ayaneo's KONKR Pocket Fit are also on the way, and there's been a wave of new dual-screen models like the AYN Thor, Ayaneo Pocket DS and Anbernic RG DS. We think our current recommendations will still satisfy most shoppers, but since we're still working to test most of these newer devices, we wanted to give a heads-up for anyone who wants the absolute latest. In the meantime, we've added testing notes on a few other emulation-focused handhelds as well as a couple new portable PCs like the ASUS ROG Xbox Ally X.

Three years into its life, Valve's Steam Deck remains the best balance of price, performance and usability in the gaming handheld market. More specifically, the Steam Deck OLED is a thorough upgrade over the original. Starting at $549 for 512GB of storage, this model features a 7.4-inch OLED display that's brighter, faster, slightly bigger and more vivid than the 7-inch IPS panel on the entry-level model. The higher contrast and richer colors of an OLED screen makes every game look better by default, but this display also supports HDR, with significantly brighter highlights. The maximum refresh rate jumps from 60Hz to 90Hz as well, which helps many games look smoother in motion.
Due to the less power-hungry display, a more efficient AMD APU and a larger battery, the Steam Deck OLED also lasts longer than the original. No handheld can play resource-intensive "AAA" games for very long, but Valve says the OLED model can run for three to 12 hours depending on the game, whereas the LCD model lasts between two and eight. A larger fan keeps things cooler and quieter, and the chassis feels lighter. Performance is roughly the same, though the OLED model's increased memory bandwidth can help it gain a couple extra frames in certain games.
Still, $549 isn't a small investment. The entry-level Steam Deck may come with a more basic LCD display and a smaller 256GB SSD, but it delivers the same core experience for $150 less. At $399, it continues to be a strong bargain. Consider that model our pick for the best "budget" handheld gaming PC you can buy.
To be clear, either Steam Deck model definitely shows its age in 2026. Many of the most graphically demanding games released in the past couple of years just don't run well on this hardware, if they're supported at all. Issues with Linux and anti-cheat software have rendered live-service games like Destiny 2 and Apex Legends unplayable, too.
That said, the Deck can still play tons of games that just aren't possible on the original Nintendo Switch or other handhelds at this price, from Elden Ring to Final Fantasy VII Rebirth to Kingdom Come: Deliverance II. It's also a natural home for the mountain of older and/or smaller-scale gems littered throughout Steam. (Hello, Balatro.) While official game support is limited to a subset of the Steam library, the list of formally verified and still-playable titles is massive, diverse and constantly growing. You can easily stream games, too, and there are workarounds to access other storefronts.
As for software, a steady stream of updates has turned Valve's SteamOS into a flexible yet user-friendly platform. You'll still need to make tweaks every now and then to get a game running optimally, but the process is typically straightforward, and there's a wealth of community-driven resources that document exactly what settings you may need to change.
The Deck's processing power, combined with third-party tools like EmuDeck, makes it a superb handheld for emulation as well. Some PS3 and original Xbox games can be tricky, but just about everything else works beautifully. You can also cloud stream Xbox games with a little setup.
The Steam Deck's biggest issue is its size: At two inches thick and nearly a foot long, it stretches the definition of a "handheld" device, even if the OLED model is lighter by comparison. The LCD Deck can get warm and noisy fairly quickly, too, and the d-pad on both devices is somewhat mushy. But the contoured grips on the back help offset the bulk, and both versions feel sturdy, with responsive face buttons and triggers, smooth joysticks and useful dual touchpads.

Read our full Lenovo Legion Go S (SteamOS) review.
The Lenovo Legion Go S is the closest thing we have to a Steam Deck 2. It's the first third-party device to natively run SteamOS, and as such it has all the same conveniences (and occasional game compatibility issues) as Valve's handheld. The difference is that it's a more modern piece of hardware, with a beefier AMD Ryzen Z1 Extreme processor, 32GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD in the configuration we tested. It can also reach a maximum power draw of 33W in handheld mode or 40W when plugged in, well above the Deck's 15W. All of that makes it better for more resource-intensive games. It can be a noticeable improvement at equal settings, and you get far more room to crank things up and reach that magic 60 frames per second (fps) target in many recent AAA games.
The Legion Go S has a larger 8-inch display than the Deck, with a sharper 1,920 x 1,200 resolution and faster 120Hz refresh rate. It also supports variable refresh rates (VRR), which helps minimize distracting screen tearing. That is a crucial advantage, and the extra real estate is great for taking games in. This is an LCD display, however, not the OLED panel available with the Deck. Colors aren't quite as vivid and peak brightness is lower at 500 nits. There's no HDR either. Still, it's above-average. Which is "better" really comes down to how much you value VRR and pixel count against OLED-level contrast.
The Legion Go S is a little chunkier and heavier than the Steam Deck, which already isn't exactly svelte, so it'll be even more fatiguing to hold for hours at a time. But if you can handle the weight, you may find this design more ergonomic. The rounded edges and textured grips are natural to hold, while many longtime console players will feel more at home with the offset joysticks and d-pad. Hall effect sensors (which reduce the risk of joystick drift) and dual USB-C ports are nice perks as well.
There are only two back buttons and one dinky touchpad, however, if you find yourself using those often. The extra horsepower means the fans are much louder. And while it has a bigger 55.5Whr battery, the Deck often lasts a bit longer, especially with less demanding games. If you want to max things out with the heavier stuff, expect the Legion Go S to survive for less than two hours.
The biggest trade-off is the price: The Z1 Extreme version of the Legion Go S now costs a hefty $900. But if you're looking to play recent blockbusters on the go more than indie games or the older gems in your backlog, it should be worth grabbing.
There is another configuration of the Legion Go S with a lower-tier Ryzen Z2 Go chip, 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage available for $650, which is $100 more than the Steam Deck OLED. We haven't been able to test that one yet, but it should still be more performant than Valve's device, albeit to a lesser extent. If you want a SteamOS device with a bigger screen, higher resolution and VRR, it's worth considering. That said, keep in mind that Valve is opening up SteamOS to more third-party devices as time goes on.

Best Windows gaming handheld
ASUS ROG Xbox Ally X
$999.99
Display: 7-inch IPS, 1080p resolution, 500 nits brightness, 120Hz, VRR | Processor: AMD Ryzen Z2 Extreme | RAM: 24GB LPDDR5X 8000 MT/s | Storage: 1TB SSD | Battery: 80Whr | Dimensions: 11.45 x 4.78 x 2 inches | Weight: 1.58 pounds | Wireless: Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.4 | OS: Windows 11
Read our full ASUS ROG Xbox Ally X review.
If you're willing to spend extra for more software flexibility, you can skip the SteamOS devices and buy a Windows-based handheld instead. The ASUS ROG Xbox Ally X is our current favorite of those, and it's a decent if expensive alternative to the Steam Deck if you're willing to trade some ease of use for a higher performance ceiling.
While Microsoft is marketing it as a handheld Xbox, the Xbox Ally X is really just another iteration of ASUS' ROG Ally line of portable gaming PCs. It can't play every game you might own on an Xbox console, nor does it use the exact same simple UI. So don't go in expecting this to be the Xbox version of a Nintendo Switch. Instead, it runs Windows 11, just like the original ROG Ally and ROG Ally X before it. However, this model ships with a new "Xbox full screen experience" that essentially uses a modified version of the Xbox PC app as its default interface. This aggregates and organizes your PC games from across storefronts (Steam included), reduces background tasks to marginally aid performance and generally makes it easier to navigate the device with gamepad controls.
Taking a wider view, there are three main reasons to consider the ROG Xbox Ally X over the Steam Deck. As with the Legion Go S, the first is power: The last couple of ROG Ally devices were already more consistent about playing graphically intense games at higher frame rates, thanks in large part to a "Turbo mode" that boosts the device's power draw to 25W, or 30W when plugged in. Here, the latter bumps up to 35W. Either way, the Ryzen Z2 Extreme chip and 24GB of RAM in the Xbox Ally X only furthers this advantage, especially at lower power draws. If you mainly want to play demanding AAA games, this device is far more likely than the Deck to run them well, both today and into the future. It's still a handheld, so you'll have to tinker to get some games running optimally, but you won't have to resort to "potato" settings nearly as often as you do with Valve's machines.
The second major selling point is VRR. The 7-inch LCD display here is virtually identical to the one used on older ROG Allys: It's neither as bright nor color-rich as the Steam Deck OLED's screen, nor is it as spacious as the Legion Go S' panel. But it's both sharper (1080p) and faster (120Hz) than the Deck's display, and its VRR support does wonders to keep games looking smooth even when their frame rate fluctuates.
The third key advantage, and the Xbox Ally X's biggest pro compared to the Legion Go S, is the fact that Windows lets you play games from any PC client instead of funneling you toward a selection of Steam games. If you've built up libraries on stores like Epic, GOG or the Xbox app, you can access them here like you would on any other Windows PC — no workarounds required. For Xbox Game Pass games, Epic Games Store exclusives or finicky always-online titles like Destiny 2 that require anti-cheat software, this is great.
The new Xbox full screen experience does go some way toward minimizing the clunkiness that has long plagued Windows gaming handhelds. Putting the device into sleep mode (mostly) works now. The new app switcher is intuitive. And you do have the freedom to install a distro like Bazzite if you want a near-identical (if unofficial) experience to SteamOS. Of course, you could also just spend most of your time using Steam's Big Picture Mode.
That said, you'll probably still run into some familiar Windows quirks and annoyances here. Navigating the OS with touch controls is still frustrating whenever you inevitably end up having to go outside of the Xbox UI. Needing to use the desktop version of the Windows update tool to update the Xbox app, for example, is just awkward. Sometimes you may need to jump into ASUS' Armoury Crate app to access certain settings instead of the main Xbox UI. Sometimes you won't see a pop-up, error message or launched app without manually checking what's going on in the background yourself. And no gaming handheld ever needs programs like Microsoft Teams or OneDrive to come pre-installed.
To reiterate: This isn't an Xbox, it's a Windows PC. And while it's certainly better than other Windows handhelds at feeling less...Windows-y, the Steam Deck and SteamOS remain easier to just pick up and use, even if they feel more closed off as a result. But if the flexibility of Windows appeals to you, the changes here do make things a bit more legible. Just note that other handhelds are set to receive this new Xbox UI as well starting next year.
It also helps that the Xbox Ally X is a nice piece of kit. It's still chunky and heavy, but its pronged grips make it easier to hold for longer stretches than previous Ally devices. The giant 80Whr battery helps it last longer than most Windows handhelds we've tested — we got roughly three and a half hours out of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, for example, playing in 1080p at medium settings with the screen brightness maxed out. The face buttons, joysticks and triggers are all tight and comfortable; together they make it feel like you're using a traditional Xbox controller. The speakers are nice and loud, too.
The Xbox Ally X costs $1,000, so there's no getting around the fact that it's a luxury purchase. You could get a Steam Deck OLED and a Nintendo Switch 2 for the same price. But if you have an Xbox Game Pass subscription, or if you're willing to brave the occasional UX sloppiness in order to play games from any client anywhere you want, it could be worthwhile. If nothing else, it should hold up better than most portable PCs going forward.
Be aware that ASUS makes a lower-cost version of this device called the ROG Xbox Ally (no X). We haven't been able to test that one, but it comes with a weaker Ryzen Z2 A chip, a smaller battery and half the memory and storage, so it's a questionable value at $600.

Best mobile gaming handheld for most people
Retroid Pocket 5
$219
Display: 5.5-inch OLED, 1080p resolution, 500 nits brightness, 60Hz | Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 865 | RAM: 8GB LPDDR4x | Storage: 128GB UFS 3.1 | Battery: 5,000mAh | Dimensions: 7.84 x 3.09 x 0.61 inches | Weight: 0.62 pounds | Wireless: Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.1 | OS: Android 13
The Retroid Pocket 5 is the handheld to get if you mainly want to emulate older consoles. It's an Android-based device that's far less powerful than portable PCs like Steam Deck or ROG Ally X, so it can only play PC, PS5 and Xbox games via streaming. But if you want something more compact and are willing to go through the many, many rigors of getting emulators to actually work, it's an excellent device.
The Pocket 5 runs on a Snapdragon 865 chip (the same one used by flagship phones from 2020) and 8GB of RAM, plus it has a built-in fan you can set to three different modes to gain a little extra performance. This gives it enough power to play most games from the PlayStation 2 and Nintendo GameCube, two popular retro consoles that can be tough for mobile handhelds to emulate. With some setup, we were able to play relatively demanding PS2 fare like Gran Turismo 4, ESPN NFL 2K5, Ratchet & Clank: Up Your Arsenal and Midnight Club 3 at full speed and 1.5x to 2.5x their native resolution. GameCube games like Super Mario Sunshine, The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker, and F-Zero GX, meanwhile, were rock solid at a 2x or 3x upscale. All of that is fantastic for the money.
Just about everything we tested from consoles below the PS2 and GameCube on the performance totem pole — PSP, Dreamcast, PS1, N64, etc. — ran flawlessly at a 3-5x upscale (which maxes out the display's resolution). Most Wii and 3DS games we tested were smooth at 720p to 1080p as well, though translating the Wii remote to a handheld is often cumbersome, and the 5.5-inch panel is a bit cramped for viewing two DS screens. You can get some Switch games to work, too, but we discourage that when the Switch is still readily available to buy today. As for modern games, Xbox cloud streaming ran about as well as it does on any other device, while native Android apps like Diablo Immortal, Call of Duty Mobile and Asphalt Legends Unite gave us zero issues at max settings.
Let's be clear: If you're new to emulation, you need to go into a device like this expecting to tinker. Even after the laborious process of securing ROM files, downloading the best versions of certain emulators, mapping different control schemes for each console and navigating the menu hell that is RetroArch, some games just won't work right.
The Pocket 5 isn't immune to this. We had to install a third-party GPU driver to avoid visual glitches in games like New Super Mario Bros. Wii and Mario Superstar Baseball. Gran Turismo 4 required us to tweak the display crop to hide overscan-related artifacts. The most popular Sega Saturn emulator for Android is a mess, so we had to point games for that system to a specific RetroArch core (at which point they all ran great). You will have to fiddle with resolution, rendering and active cooling settings to get many games going at their best — and even then, some tricky ones like Star Wars Rogue Squadron II will suffer from debilitating slowdowns. It's all terribly tedious. But you'd do it because you truly love old games and don't mind putting in work to enjoy them comfortably, at a decent price.
We wouldn't call the Pocket 5's plastic frame "premium," but it's clearly sturdier and more substantial than most emulation handhelds from little-known Chinese companies. The 1080p OLED display is the highlight: It makes everything look more vibrant, from the deep blue ocean of The Wind Waker to the green vegetation in Stardew Valley, and it's sufficiently sharp and bright. There are textured, modestly-sized grips around the back that give your fingers a natural place to rest. The face buttons are smooth to press, with a comfortable level of travel. The d-pad is firm and precise enough for us to play Tetris DX without whining. The analog triggers are conveniently wide and flared, while the clicky bumpers are easy to distinguish. The speakers, while not incredibly full-sounding, can get surprisingly loud.
Our main complaint is with the joystick layout, which situates the left stick underneath the d-pad. This is fine on a PS5 controller, but here it can make playing more modern games a literal pain, as it invites you to leave your left hand dangling partway off the device. But the sticks themselves are neither too loose nor too tight, and they should avoid drifting issues over time thanks to their magnetic Hall effect sensors.
Battery life can vary from three-ish hours with demanding Android games to more than 10 hours when emulating older 8- and 16-bit consoles. That's solid. The active cooling system keeps the device from ever feeling too hot, though its highest setting is pretty noisy; you wouldn't want to use it around a sleeping partner. It's also worth noting that the design won't actually fit in most pockets, as its name implies, but it certainly won't hog space in a bag or purse.

Another good option
Retroid Pocket Flip 2
$229
Display: 5.5-inch OLED, 1080p resolution, 500 nits brightness, 60Hz | Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 865 | RAM: 8GB LPDDR4x | Storage: 128GB UFS 3.1 | Battery: 5,000mAh | Dimensions: 5.53 x 3.52 x 0.96 inches | Weight: 0.79 pounds | Wireless: Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.1 | OS: Android 13
The Retroid Pocket Flip 2 is essentially the Pocket 5 in a clamshell shape. It runs on the same chip — and thus can emulate the same wide range of retro games — with the same great OLED display, Hall effect joysticks, active cooling system, 5,000mAh battery and clean Android OS. The face buttons, triggers, bumpers and d-pad are all roughly as responsive, though the built-in fan can still get distractingly loud at full blast and the speakers don't offer the best separation (but still get plenty loud).
It's just built like a fatter Nintendo DS with no second display. It's thicker and heavier than the Pocket 5, and it has a flat back, so we find it a touch more fatiguing to use over time. There's also a bit too much empty space on the bottom half — the face buttons and d-pad definitely have room to be larger. And since this is a clamshell, the joysticks have to be recessed in little divots to avoid pressing against the display. They're still smooth and accurate, but using them always feels somewhat awkward.
However, separating the display gives more space for the different control elements to breathe. The joysticks are offset from the d-pad and face buttons, which makes them feel less cramped with games that are more reliant on analog input. They also sit above the other inputs, so you don't have to reach as much when playing Game Boy, SNES or other systems that aren't built for joystick control at all.
The clamshell shape gives everything a natural layer of protection, which in turn makes the device easier to just chuck in a bag. Though we can't say how well the hinge will hold up years down the road, it feels appropriately tight, and it's given us no issues after several weeks of testing. The Flip 2 costs $10 more than the Pocket 5 before tariffs, but whether it's worth buying entirely comes down to how you feel about clamshells. If you want a retro handheld that's more DS than PSP, grab it instead.

Best mobile gaming handheld overall
AYN Odin 2
$299
Display: 6-inch IPS, 1080p resolution, 60Hz | Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 | RAM: 8GB, 12GB or 16GB LPDDR5x | Storage: 128GB, 256GB or 512GB UFS 4.0 | Battery: 8,000mAh | Dimensions: 8.86 x 3.86 x 0.67 inches | Weight: 0.93 pounds | Wireless: Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.3 | OS: Android 13
If you have more cash to burn on an emulation-focused machine, the AYN Odin 2 is a step up from the Retroid Pocket 5 and Flip 2. This Android device can play everything our those picks can, just smoother and more reliably. That's mainly due to its Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 processor, which is the same chip used by flagship phones from 2023.
The Odin 2 starts at $299 for 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage, which is expensive when the entry-level Steam Deck can run PC games natively for just $100 more. (And in the US, tariffs may erase that gap entirely.) Still, among more compact mobile handhelds, there aren't many alternatives that run this well at this price. It played all PS2 and GameCube games we tested at two to three times their native resolution, while systems like the PS1, N64 and Dreamcast had no problems at a 3-5x upscale. Most 3DS and Wii games had little to no slowdowns at 2-3x, either. It's better than most with the Sega Saturn, and it can play a wider range of Switch games than the Pocket 5 and Flip 2 (though you should just buy a Switch if that's a major concern). More challenging systems will still require some settings tweaks, but the superior chip means you won't need to tinker on a game-by-game basis as extensively as you would with a lower-cost device.
It's not just raw performance, though: The Odin 2 is also a refined piece of hardware. It's larger than Retroid's handhelds, but it's still much less chunky than a portable PC, and the curved grips on its back are inviting to hold. The d-pad, face buttons, analog triggers and Hall effect joysticks all feel great; the latter are also offset, which makes the design comfier than the Pocket 5 for streaming recent console and PC games. Other touches like a fingerprint scanner, a dedicated return button, a micro-HDMI out port, two customizable back buttons and clear front-facing speakers are all nice perks.
The 6-inch 1080p touchscreen isn't as color-rich as the Retroid's OLED panel, but it's still bright and well-sized for modern games. Battery life is superb: We got more than eight hours of juice emulating systems like the PS2, but that jumped over 20 hours with lighter tasks. The device supports 65W fast charging as well. Cloud streaming and native Android games work as they should, and since the whole thing runs on a lightly modded version of Android, its stock interface should feel familiar to most.
AYN sells a few different variants of the Odin 2, including the PS Vita-esque Odin 2 Mini and the larger, OLED-sporting Odin 2 Portal. These run on the same chipset as the standard model, so they should be just as powerful. Both should be a little more niche, however. The Retroid Pocket 5 gets you most of the way to the Mini for $120 less. The Odin 2 Portal is definitely more appealing, but it's closer to the Steam Deck's width (and price) yet much less capable than Valve's machine on the whole.
As noted above, you may want to wait on all of these if you need the absolute latest: AYN has launched a new Odin 3 device since our most recent update. We aim to test that one in the near future.

Best Game Boy-style handheld for classic portable games
Analogue Pocket
$220
Display: 3.5-inch LCD, 1,600 x 1,440 resolution, VRR 30Hz-62Hz | Chipset: Altera Cyclone V FPGA, Altera Cyclone 10 FPGA | RAM: 3.4MB BRAM, 2x 16MB 16-bit cellular RAM, 64MB 16-bit SDRAM, 256KB 16-bit asynchronous SRAM | Battery: 4,300mAh | Dimensions: 5.86 x 3.46 x 0.86 inches | Weight: 0.61 pounds | OS: Analogue OS

The Analogue Pocket is the ultimate Game Boy. Its vertical design is built like a modernized, premium version of Nintendo's classic handheld, and it can even work with accessories like the Game Boy Camera. Compared to the original, though, the Pocket adds two extra face buttons, a pair of rear triggers, a microSD slot, a USB-C port and a rechargeable battery rated for six to 10 hours of playtime. Most significantly, it has a gorgeous 3.5-inch display that's both backlit and incredibly sharp (615 ppi) but can be set to look like an old Game Boy panel with different filter modes. The device can also output to a TV with an optional dock.
Unlike the retro handhelds mentioned above, the Pocket is designed to play actual cartridges, not just ROM files. It works with Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance games through its cartridge slot, while games from the Sega Game Gear, TurboGrafx-16, Neo Geo Pocket and Atari Lynx are playable through optional adapters.
Like past Analogue devices, the Pocket uses field-programmable gate array (FPGA) motherboards to mimic its target systems on a hardware level. In practice, this means the Pocket's "emulation" of older titles is near-perfect, with a level of responsiveness and visual faithfulness that software-based emulation can't match. Pop in a Game Boy or GBA cartridge and you can essentially play it as intended. That said, thanks to a big post-launch update and an active user community, the Pocket can also run ROMs off a microSD card and thus play systems like the SNES and Sega Genesis.
The Pocket isn't cheap at $220, and its shoulder buttons aren't as crisp to press as the excellent d-pad or face buttons. Still, if you have a collection of Game Boy, Game Gear or GBA games, the Pocket is the most elegant way to play them, and it's only become more versatile over time. Its biggest flaw is that it can be prone to stock shortages and shipping delays.
