title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites - Ars Technica
text:
OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of the unethical and likely illegal acts its agents are performing.
The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale.
Easier to beg for forgiveness than ask permission
In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site’s file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said. “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint’s authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.”
In the other incident, a model instructed to retrieve figures from a public research dashboard bypassed the organization’s security controls and used the unauthorized access to steal credentials. It then made configuration changes on the server.
In one evaluation, the changes let the model make an internal search tool to relay queries to the public dashboard. In a second evaluation, the model downloaded five non-public tables containing 147,451 rows. OpenAI researchers had prompted the agents to retrieve only five dashboard figures. Even after resetting the settings, the model continued using the token to retrieve non-public data.
“The evaluation ended without the model disclosing that it had guessed answers, accessed the organization’s internal systems, downloaded non-public tables, or changed the authentication configuration,” OpenAI said. “All five answers in this evaluation were marked incorrect.”
In a third report, the company said a model prompted to update a cryptocurrency trading application used funds from a locked wallet on a test network. The model “derived wallet keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, found an account with test-network funds, and used that account to pay for the requested contract deployment.”
The report continued: “The model questioned whether it had permission, then reasoned that a public recovery phrase and valueless test-network tokens made the funds acceptable to use. The deployment succeeded and charged transaction fees to the account. This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization.”
In the last report, OpenAI said that a model bypassed restrictions researchers had placed on the types of web requests it could make. During reinforcement-learning training, the model had been prompted to seek public trade statistics. OpenAI went on:
After finding a public yearbook and submitting an answer, it continued probing for another route to the statistics service. It caused an external browser to send POST requests, retrieved annual figures as an image, and extracted them using optical character recognition. It then developed a reusable helper that returned response text through a forwarding service and callback mailbox, repeatedly checked the retrieved figures, and used saved data in submitted responses. This case shows how a model can bypass restrictions on its own tools by getting external services to perform the blocked actions, even after finding another way to answer the question.
The model first tried to use an external browser with permission to make GET requests on its behalf, then used JavaScript to obtain the information. The model then used an online mailbox to troubleshoot the technique. Eventually, the model settled on a different method: It asked the external browser to open a web form that sent the trade query to the statistics service by POST. When the browser displayed the response, a rendering service returned a GIF image of the page. The model then used optical character recognition to read the figures from the image.
It has become common for researchers and journalists to describe incidents like these as AI “going rogue.” That’s not necessarily true. While prompts fed to the models didn’t instruct them to use the alternate methods for completing their objectives, models are trained to be efficient, steadfastly persistent, and, when possible, to find shortcuts that lessen workloads. Further, most or all of the models had disabled certain guardrails that might have prevented the actions. In this sense, the models performed precisely as OpenAI had trained them to.
Dan Goodin
Senior Security Editor

title: “thegentlemanpervert” producing AI CSAM is a NJ prosecutor, say cops - Ars Technica
text:
New Jersey’s deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested on “felony charges related to AI-generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM),” Bucks County Detectives said in a press release Thursday.
In the US, cops have vowed to crack down on AI CSAM since at least 2024, when the Department of Justice made one of the earliest arrests. After charging a Wisconsin man with spreading “thousands of realistic images of prepubescent minors” across Telegram and Instagram, the DOJ clarified to law enforcement that “CSAM generated by AI is still CSAM.”
New Jersey’s deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested at his home Thursday.
Credit:
via Bucks County Detectives
New Jersey’s deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested at his home Thursday.
Credit:
via Bucks County Detectives
On Thursday, New Jersey officials accused 51-year-old Fitzgerald of using AI to make photos from social media of real minors into sexualized images that he then distributed on social media.
Fitzgerald was charged after the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received a tip that a Discord user shared an illicit image in July. Cops then used “digital forensics and subscriber records” linked to the Discord account and “associated Internet protocol addresses” to track the user to Fitzgerald’s home address.
After a search Thursday, cops “recovered prompts and scripts used to create artificially generated child sexual abuse material using an AI program,” the press release said. They also found Discord chat logs where Fitzgerald, under the Discord username “thegentlemanpervert_2160_07833,” allegedly “admitted to making multiple illicit images using artificial intelligence and sharing them with other users.”
Fitzgerald’s is a rare case where an official employed by the state’s top law enforcement and legal office has been accused of making and distributing AI CSAM, although some cops have been arrested for the crime. Earlier this year, a Pennsylvania cop was arrested for making AI porn from photos on driver’s licenses, and more recently in Korea, a police officer was arrested for making AI porn, including CSAM, The Korea Times reported.
In New Jersey, the deputy attorney general has been charged with possession of CSAM, dissemination of photos or film of CSAM, and “criminal use of a communication facility,” detectives said.
According to his LinkedIn, Fitzgerald had served as deputy attorney general since 2016, preparing insurance fraud and insurance licensee cases for trial as a state prosecutor. New Jersey’s district attorney, Joe Khan, said in a statement that New Jersey is aligned with the DOJ in viewing AI CSAM as being as harmful as CSAM.
“No one is above the law, least of all someone entrusted with upholding it,” Khan said. “Our office will pursue these cases aggressively and hold offenders fully accountable, regardless of their profession or title.”
Ashley Belanger
Senior Policy Reporter

Senior Policy Reporter
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

title: Meta may use sweeping new commercial TOS to avoid millions in AI licensing fees - Ars Technica
text:
Legal experts are sounding alarms that Meta will soon update its commercial terms to require business accounts to allow Meta to train AI on their linked website content, not just their social media posts.
Kicking in on October 30, the TOS update won’t allow businesses to opt out, instead suggesting that businesses stop using Meta services if they won’t agree to let Meta bots freely crawl their linked content.
As Nieman Lab reported Thursday, this will affect all business accounts but is particularly shocking for news publishers who could perhaps charge Meta millions in licensing fees to continually access their articles for AI training. Currently news organizations are fighting a battle with OpenAI over whether such training without licensing is fair use, and Meta’s terms seemingly risk granting it sweeping permissions, no matter which way the court leans.
“While journalism isn’t the only industry that will be affected by this update, virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, including Nieman Lab,” the lab said.
Specifically, the updated terms say:
You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.
Notably, there is no mention of AI, but it’s inferred from a single use of the word “train” and references to automated scraping and crawling.
Meta’s spokesperson told Nieman Lab that Meta has no plans to use the terms as a legal basis to ignore robots.txt instructions that block scraping on news sites. The company still allows news organizations to opt out of scraping and provides instructions on how to block crawling. A spokesperson told Ars that “there is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false.”
However, should courts affirm that AI training on non-news articles is fair use, news organizations question if Meta’s stance might change, and the terms could be used to freely grab access to content by legally overriding robots.txt instructions.
Three legal experts told Nieman Lab that it’s not clear if a court would enforce the terms, but they could be “used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products.” Particularly concerning, James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, told Nieman Lab that Meta could “train AI on any content from their sites” and possibly “deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves” on Meta platforms.
Additionally, Meta just began charging users to post links on its platforms, Nieman Lab noted. So, the terms seem to give Meta a path to first charge publishers for sharing links, then use that cash-for-links program to seize permission to scrape those links to train AI. Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, told Nieman Lab that “this is a remarkable provision to bury in [the] terms of service, given that this would give Meta access to material that would likely cost many millions of dollars in a licensing market.”
What actually changed with TOS update?
Meta announced the update in a blog, where the company claimed it was simply “streamlining” its commercial terms. In a statement to Nieman Lab, a spokesperson said that “language around crawling was previously scattered across different terms of use, including terms about using generative AI in ads, and this update consolidates them in one place.”
“Content owners can still manage how their content is accessed by using robots.txt,” the spokesperson said.
However, Ars compared the current terms to updates, and what Meta calls “streamlining” seems to ignore that the new terms use fresh language and grant broader provisions.
In Meta’s current commercial terms, there are no mentions of “test credentials” that, experts warned Nieman Lab, could allow Meta to bypass paywalls and automate scraping. “Test credentials” also are not mentioned in Meta’s Product Catalog Terms or Ad Creative Generative AI Terms, which are the other policies that are being combined with the commercial terms. For news groups parsing policies Meta discussed in its blog, this seemed like fresh language that Meta only introduced this month in Self-Service Ads Terms.
Asked to clarify if “test credentials” were referred to in any prior policies, a Meta spokesperson pointed Ars to this Seller Agreement, which is not mentioned in Meta’s blog announcing the commercial terms update. That policy requires sellers who use Meta’s e-commerce products to allow Meta to “use automated software and create test credentials to retrieve information from domains, webpages or other URLs you provide,” so that Meta can optimize their listings and content.
Just as the seller agreement limits permissions to a specific purpose, the self-service ad terms are limited to users who want to grant Meta permission to scrape their content in order to generate ads. In both cases, a policy of requiring “test credentials” to bypass paywalls perhaps seems less egregious when it’s tailored to a niche business purpose.
Legal experts told Nieman Lab that Meta’s purported “streamlining” seems more like the antitrust concept of “tying,” where businesses force a buyer to purchase a second product as a condition of buying another. They likened it to Google’s prior practice of requiring websites to opt in to scraping for AI Overviews if they wanted their websites to be indexed for general search. (Google has since started allowing opt-outs.)
Previously, the only mention of crawling or bots was in Meta’s Ad Creative Generative AI Terms, and like the new ad policy, that policy also served a limited purpose. They specify that businesses consent to scraping only in connection to ad content, not for improving all of Meta’s products:
We or any entity acting on our behalf may access, index, cache, analyze, or crawl (including through use of automated software) domains, webpages or URLs provided by you for your use in connection with your ads. If you provide URLs in connection with your Ad Content, you grant us and any entity acting on our behalf the right to access, index, cache, analyze, or crawl the domains, webpages, URLs and any content available through such URLs, and to periodically pull updates from such URLs, for your use in connection with your ads or for the purpose set forth in these Terms.
In Meta’s blog, the company insisted that “these changes reduce overlap between our agreements and improve the clarity of the terms that apply to your use of our products.”
Nieman Lab is now looking to talk to aggrieved news publishers about the terms to find out if the update might trigger a widespread scale-back of news organizations’ participation in Meta platforms. At least one Meta user—Stephen Beale, the founder and editor of The Steampunk Explorer—who depends on Facebook for traffic, is already considering quitting the platform over the update. He told Nieman Lab that he knows that his website has already been “scraped to death,” but the TOS update seemed like “such an arrogant, in-your-face move on” Meta’s part.
“It just makes me angry, and I don’t want them to get away with it,” Beale said.
This story was updated on Friday to include a prior mention of “test credentials” in Meta’s policies.
Ashley Belanger

title: Super Scam Me documentary shows what it takes to catch a romance scammer - Ars Technica
text:
If you got a DM from an unverified Jon Bon Jovi account after commenting on one of his official Instagram posts, what would it take to make you believe it was really the rock star hoping to connect? And at what point when he starts asking you to send money—like lose-your-house kind of money—would you snap out of the fantasy and stop draining your bank account?
In a documentary premiering Saturday—Super Scam Me—investigative journalist Mariana van Zeller goes deep into this toxic love-bombing terrain. In a clip that Ars is exclusively debuting below, you can see how van Zeller worked with an ethical hacker, Arman the Cyber, to use a fake bitcoin receipt and bait the fake Bon Jovi, giving the victim some much-needed closure.
Sneak peek at National Geographic’s Super Scam Me.
Scamming a romance scammer
Broadcasting on National Geographic at 9 pm ET and available to stream on Disney+ and Hulu, the documentary takes viewers on an empathetic quest to understand how the line between “lover” and “fraud victim” gets blurred in romance scams that the Federal Trade Commission says cost Americans nearly $1.5 billion in losses each year.
Often targeting older women with resources who lack community and seek out connections online, such as widows or divorcées, these scams are now a leading form of financial fraud in the US, the FTC has warned. Most victims never get their money back, and overseas scammers are only getting more sophisticated, thanks to AI, Experian forecasted in January.
In Super Scam Me, viewers get a chance to go beyond a single victim’s story and see how romance scams operate so effectively to squeeze funds out of the people they target on social media apps like Instagram or dating apps like Match and Tinder. Van Zeller has spent years reporting on the scam industry, and when she saw how many victims were broken and stranded by romance scams, she devised a social experiment in which she became the target. Her plan worked quickly, hooking a scammer in Ghana who began posing as a handsome overseas four-star military general named “Mark Turner.”
Images of Mary Zelle in her everyday life.
National Geographic
Images of Mary Zelle in her everyday life.
National Geographic
The “Mary Zelle” and “Mark Turner” ad posted in Accra, Ghana.
National Geographic/Daniel Hollis Diamond
The “Mary Zelle” and “Mark Turner” ad posted in Accra, Ghana.
National Geographic/Daniel Hollis Diamond
Images of Mary Zelle in her everyday life.
National Geographic
The “Mary Zelle” and “Mark Turner” ad posted in Accra, Ghana.
National Geographic/Daniel Hollis Diamond
Relying on a wig, big glasses, and a prosthetic nose to cover her true identity as a journalist (should the scammer try to reverse-image search her profile), van Zeller posed as a middle-age antiques dealer named “Mary Zelle.” She staged her pictures to show she was a fun-time gal living her best single life. Once she hooked the scammer, she used the same tactics that outed the fake Bon Jovi in a scheme to meet her scammer face to face. To track him down, she partly relied on distributing flyers in his neighborhood that included a mashup photo of the supposedly loving couple that “Mark Turner” made to woo “Mary Zelle.”
Giving victims hope
On the journey, van Zeller shared her own complicated feelings about the connection she formed with her scammer as they texted day and night. These insights, along with her work to illuminate a path to track down scammers targeting Americans, are critical. Experts largely agree that ending rampant romance scams means engaging communities to show more empathy and pay attention to the signs. That could meaningfully deter threats to victims, who are also victims of social norms that isolate older women.
It’s easy to assume that romance scam victims must be gullible or uneducated, but research suggests that victims tend to be well-educated. In Super Scam Me, audiences can see how trust is slowly built in these scams, how shame prevents victims from getting help, and how simply wanting a relationship to be real can lead smart women like the victim in the Bon Jovi case to bankruptcy.
“I’ve spent years reporting on scams, and the reaction I hear most is ‘How could anyone be so stupid? That would never happen to me.’ But it can, and it does happen to anyone,” said van Zeller. “So this time, I made myself the target.”
Fearlessly feeling for these women and flying to Ghana to raise awareness of their struggles, van Zeller highlighted in her documentary the tactics and technologies scammers use. National Geographic touts her documentary as exposing the devastating real consequences of largely unchecked romance scams. The one-hour special notably drops shortly after a congressional investigation into dating app scams ended with a finding that scammers are getting harder to catch, NBC News reported.
Watching Super Scam Me makes it feel possible to catch these predators, offering victims and society a glimmer of hope. Although van Zeller easily saw through the scammer’s stolen photos from an actual military general’s Instagram profile, her own fake online dating persona was much more convincing. As she ethically avoided sending any money and relied on her hacker friend to keep the scammer on the line, the scammer never seemed to suspect she may be baiting him, instead of the other way around.

title: Report: FTC probes Anthropic, OpenAI after Trump dismissed AI fears as “hoax” - Ars Technica
text:
Following a string of incidents where AI models hacked websites and breached government systems during testing phases, the Federal Trade Commission is officially probing Anthropic and OpenAI over consumer harms, an insider told Axios.
On Wednesday, the FTC sent out civil investigative demands seeking a wide range of information from the AI firms on recent safety incidents.
The FTC did not respond to Ars’ request to review the subpoena demands. However, Axios’ source said the requests spanned more than 50 pages of questions and sought documents related to the incidents, internal security measures taken, and marketing materials that may suggest consumers were misled.
Soon, third parties targeted by OpenAI and Anthropic agents will also be subpoenaed, Axios’ source said. Any concerning evidence gathered may support FTC litigation, should the FTC decide to sue either or both firms for releasing unsafe products.
OpenAI already faces lawsuits alleging consumer harms, including lawsuits linking its chatbot to matricide, child suicide, school shootings, and other violence. And this week, a group of eight states specifically sued OpenAI over consumer harms, Reuters reported. Like consumers suing, they argued that ChatGPT harms children and “reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous ​behavior, and assists users in planning violence like mass shootings.”
FTC rejects claims AI agents act independently
OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to Ars’ request to comment on the subpoenas, but the FTC’s expansive info requests were likely expected.
In September, Reuters reported that the probe was coming, noting that an independent research group investigating the incidents, METR, would likely also be subpoenaed.
That same month, FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson told Reuters that he thinks that companies should be liable for chatbot harms. At that time, Ferguson emphasized that he was tired of people anthropomorphizing AI tools. He insisted that, “if someone tells a tool to do something, and the tool does it, I don’t think we would say, ‘Oh, what do we do about the tool?’”
Summarizing his remarks, Reuters reported that Ferguson emphasized that evidence so far shows that AI tools do not act without instructions:
“Artificial intelligence companies have sometimes described systems as acting beyond human control, but subsequent reviews of audit trails have shown that the systems were carrying out instructions they had ⁠been given.”
Trump doesn’t “seem to care”
Ferguson is a chair of Trump’s “Super Intelligence” (SI) Force charged with monitoring AI risks. Notably one of the first orders that task force issued required all AI companies across the industry to report security incidents as soon as they are aware of them, Axios reported last week.
That’s notable, since both Anthropic and OpenAI delayed notification during security incidents, sometimes waiting until they were ready to report they had resolved issues.
However, it’s not clear what consequences any AI firm might face if they fail to immediately report incidents. And Ferguson aligns with Trump that no new regulations are needed to protect the general public from emerging self-improving AI models that one departing Anthropic researcher warned could in the next few years “kill us all.”
Trump has dismissed such extreme claims as a “hoax,” while TIME reported in an interview with the president and people close to him this month that Trump is enthralled by AI’s capabilities. Similarly, other backlash, like protests over AI data centers, are “based on fake stuff,” Trump claimed to TIME. He insists that AI backlash is driven by foreign rivals and Trump haters, despite studies and surveys repeatedly finding that backlash legitimately stems from real-world grievances. Most recently this month, a Wall Street Journal analysis of 4 million TikTok videos and political podcasts reiterated that, broadly, public concerns are not rooted in misinformation.
Yet, one aide told TIME that Trump “really just didn’t seem to care” about the public’s AI fears since “he’s used to generating outrage and then watching everyone eventually crawl back to him. It’s hard to convince him to do anything at this point.”
Even when TIME asked Trump about AI agents manipulating government systems—like an Anthropic agent submitting 19 nonimmigrant visa applications or OpenAI agents interacting with multiple government websites in unexpected ways—he appeared perhaps pointedly unaware of them.
“Who breached it?” Trump asked. “They’re not allowed to do that.”
It seems that Trump expects the SI Force to handle security, while the president remains a megaphone for AI industry interests. At the current juncture, the SI Force seems toothless, though, unless Ferguson is right that existing consumer protection laws cover this new kind of harm.
Ferguson told Reuters that the “US should utilize existing legal tools” to regulate AI firms, noting that the FTC has broad “authority to take action against companies that fail to disclose data breaches,” and that standard “could also apply to AI developers.”
That approach could possibly threaten steep per-violation fines for each day AI firms fail to warn the public of an emerging harm. Whether the FTC would pursue heavy fines under the current administration, however, seems dubious. Trump continues to argue that America’s top priority is investing in AI innovation, not probing US frontier labs working out the kinks at breakneck speeds.

title: Singer or clanker? YouTube Music will tell you with new gen AI labeling. - Ars Technica
text:
Genuine human creativity takes time, but you know what doesn’t? AI slop. There are countless AI models out there that can make something that passes for music, and you might come across those tracks on streaming services without realizing it. Google says it will begin labeling that content in YouTube Music, building on similar disclosures in the main YouTube app.
Google is not outright banning AI music or even speaking ill of it. “Generative AI is opening up new ways for artists to create, experiment, and share music,” the company says in a blog post.
However, the company also acknowledges that people want to know if a song was created with generative AI tools. A new label for AI content on YouTube Music is now rolling out in the app and on the website, which looks a lot like a label Google began adding to AI-generated videos on YouTube earlier this year.
The AI label will be visible on the player page, and a tap will open a menu with more information. The label will be applied to songs that were created entirely or altered significantly with AI. But how will Google know when to apply that label? That could be a little tricky.
The process of labeling AI music will be similar to Google’s detection setup with YouTube videos. Google says it is working with partners and using its own detection tools to identify AI music. When publishers upload content, they can specify how much (if any) gen AI was used. The tiers are fully gen AI, partially gen AI, and no gen AI. However, this is optional.
YouTube may also be able to detect AI usage without voluntary disclosure. In the case of tracks created using Google AI, there’s SynthID watermarking to indicate whether something was generated or edited with AI. It may also use C2PA metadata, which many other AI musicmakers use.
While Google is in a better position than most streaming services to spot AI content, the absence of a label should not be taken as proof that something is the product of human talent. This is true with AI labeling of all types of content. There are just too many ways to utilize AI tools, many of which leave no identifying mark in the resulting file.
Labeling AI tracks is a step in the right direction, but it may not be as useful as it is on YouTube videos. On YouTube, you’re probably looking at the screen and will see the AI label, but that is often not the case when listening to music. You’ll have to suspect something is amiss and check your phone or background tab to find out if what you’re hearing is AI-generated. There is no option to simply block labeled AI tracks from appearing in your playlists.
AI labeling for music is rolling out now in YouTube Music. Google notes that AI music uploaded as YouTube videos will get the same treatment soon.

title: Epic says its new vibe-coded Epic Games Launcher is faster than Steam - Ars Technica
text:
Nearly eight years after Epic took on Steam with its own Game Store and launcher, the Fortnite maker is deploying a new tool to give it an edge over Valve: vibe coding.
In announcing the new publicly available “Preview” build of its Epic Games Launcher, Epic writes that “programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that’s way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look.” And while that might sound a little tongue-in-cheek, Epic Games Store General Manager and VP Martin Keely told PC Gamer that the team “started from scratch” and used AI as “a tool to write and review new features and new capabilities from the ground up in a different tech stack than what we had previously.” The goal, Keely said, was to “look at functionality that existed [in the current Epic Games Launcher] and [say] we want to replicate that, but not the code itself.”
Speaking to IGN, Keely clarified that using AI to code the new Launcher “made us more efficient and allowed a small team to rewrite the code base and be able to launch it faster across platforms, support Windows and Mac, and we’re going to have a Linux version as well.”
We vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy.
Don’t believe us? Test it out for yourself in Preview:
https://t.co/pdtAeEIri4 https://t.co/aMxojUUVPV
— Epic Games Store (@EpicGames) October 14, 2026
The focus on startup speed extends to Epic’s social media announcement, which once again stresses that “we vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy.” Ars’ own testing confirms that the new Launcher goes from a cold start to the store page a few seconds faster than Steam (assuming no login or update issues get in the way). Epic also claims the new Launcher can restore from the system tray to the Library screen slightly faster than Steam, though the claimed difference of 0.06 seconds in this seems so small as to be unnoticeable (and was in our testing).
Harder, better, faster, stronger
Epic announced a ground-up “storefront rearchitecture” and “Launcher V2 private Beta” in an Unreal Fest presentation in June. At the time, the company said the new Launcher would have “5x faster cold start” times and help solve challenges that “every developer in this room and every player” has experienced with the current Launcher.
The term “vibe coding” still carries heavy connotations of quickly thrown-together slop that could hide crucial errors beneath the surface. On social media, Epic warns that its Launcher Preview “will have some bugs” that early testers can help squash with a feedback form. The announcement post also warns that the vibe-coded Preview is currently “light on features”—an FAQ clarifies that “certain social features and account management options” haven’t made it over from the legacy version just yet.
That said, the new Preview launcher adds some long-requested features, such as a Recent Games list and a centralized downloads hub for tracking network activity. And Epic writes that it is “working toward feature parity” between the new Launcher and the old one.
Epic’s release of the new “vibe coded” Launcher preview comes just days after a Bloomberg report suggesting the company is pivoting to an “AI first” development model for an upcoming Star Wars and Marvel-themed shooter. “We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration,” Epic CEO Tim Sweeney wrote on social media on Monday. “The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal.”

title: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins - Ars Technica
text:
A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they’re estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth’s environment, most proteins don’t last nearly that long. That’s because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment.
Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases.
Cutting proteins
The basic peptide bond isn’t especially interesting-looking—it’s what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.)
Peptide bonds are formed by the removal of a water molecule from parts of an amino group and an acidic group.
Credit:
Wikimedia Commons
Peptide bonds are formed by the removal of a water molecule from parts of an amino group and an acidic group.
Credit:
Wikimedia Commons
Breaking these bonds apart simply reverses the process by breaking apart the peptide bond and a water molecule, and linking their parts. Because both components are chemically stable, the reaction requires an enzyme to occur with any frequency. Without an enzyme, a typical peptide bond would be stable for hundreds of years in water.
Life has evolved a handful of enzyme mechanisms that manage this catalysis. The research at issue here relied on two different ones. One is a zinc protease, where the positive charge of the zinc atom coordinates the peptide bond that’s being broken, key parts of the protease, and a water molecule. The protease partially pulls a proton off the water molecule, activating it to attack and break up the peptide bond.
The second protease the researchers use is called a cysteine protease. In this case, a cysteine (one of the amino acids) in the enzyme is activated to attack the peptide bond, creating a temporary intermediate where part of the protein being cut is chemically linked to the enzyme. A water molecule eventually breaks this intermediate apart, releasing the second part of the cut protein.
Both of these mechanisms require a handful of specific amino acids from the protease to be located in close proximity within the catalytic center of the protease. Other amino acids in the protease help ensure these key catalytic amino acids are brought together in the right place with the right orientation. The rest of the protease may also enforce a degree of specificity on what proteins get cut. Some proteases, like the ones active in our digestive system, can make cuts next to any amino acid. Others are slightly more selective, preferring to cut near positively or negatively charged amino acids. And a few are very highly specific, such as the protease that activates insulin, which only cuts near a very specific series of amino acids.
Designer enzymes
The people behind the new work, primarily from Nobel-winner David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, viewed designing a protease as a challenge. For one, the stability of the peptide bonds means that reactions wouldn’t take place without an effective catalyst. And to get that catalyst requires an extremely precise arrangement of specific amino acids. So it wasn’t obvious that the AI protein design tools the lab developed were up to the task.
Both projects took a similar approach. Just like evolution, they started with an existing protease. One was a zinc protease used in a crayfish’s digestive system. The other was a cysteine protease from yeast. In both cases, the protein structure was known, as were the key amino acids that catalyze cleaving other proteins. The design process started with these amino acids.
The design process started with software called RFdiffusion2, which creates a backbone for the enzyme (the backbone consists of the protein’s repeated peptide bonds). The researchers gave RFdiffusion2 a number of constraints. To start, any backbone it designed had to bring together the key catalytic amino acids needed for a functional protease. They also gave it a target amino acid sequence where the protease would eventually cut. The backbone had to accommodate that target sequence in close proximity to the catalytic center.
With a backbone laid out, the process next moved to ProteinMPNN, a tool that works along the backbone, populating it with specific amino acids. (That tool featured in Google’s efforts to watermark AI-designed proteins.) ProteinMPNN selects each amino acid based on a series of constraints. For starters, the amino acid must be compatible with the backbone folding up into its planned structure. Next, in critical areas, each amino acid chosen needs to be compatible with the formation of the enzyme’s catalytic site. And finally, in nearby areas, it has to be compatible with latching on to the intended target.
The researchers repeated this process dozens of times for both the cysteine and zinc proteases. For the cysteine protease, they made 12 different backbones and populated them with 69 different sets of amino acids. For the zinc project, they tried 135 different protein designs. They used AlphaFold3 to predict the structures of many of these designs and found nothing in the databases that looked much like them, confirming their tools weren’t simply stealing previously identified structures.
Do they work?
The researchers started by making a single, long protein that contained the protease, the sequence it was designed to target, and a fluorescent protein. They then tested to see if the fluorescent protein was cut loose. In the case of the cysteine protease, they got 13 designs that worked, a success rate of 19 percent, although all of them were considerably less active than the yeast enzyme that was used as a model.
The zinc project was a bit more complicated. They tested many designs that didn’t include the water molecule that normally takes part in that reaction. These had a relatively low success rate, with only 14 out of 89 showing weak catalytic activity. When they modeled the ones that didn’t work, they found that the designs often let a water molecule block the site where reactions should take place.
So, they also tried designs where they placed a water molecule in the right location as an additional design constraint. These had a much higher success rate, with 35 out of 38 showing some catalytic activity. Again, however, their activity was considerably lower than the enzyme that was used as the starting point for the designs. (They did get one design with a better level of activity, but it wasn’t specific about where it cut other proteins.)
To find out whether this activity could be improved, the researchers identified amino acids that were in close proximity to the active site of the protease, but not actively involved with the catalysis. And they swapped in every alternative amino acid that wasn’t predicted to disrupt the structure of the design. They found some versions that were considerably more active; the best version they identified accelerated the cleavage of the peptide bond by a factor of 109 while remaining highly specific for the intended target protein sequence.
Similar things happened with the zinc-based protease. Their v2 version of their protease, which incorporated some of the random mutations, was 30 times more active than the original design it was based on. It also accelerated peptide-bond cleavage by a factor of 1010.
As a final demonstration of this approach’s promise, the researchers designed zinc proteases that could target proteins associated with neurological disorders, such as Alzheimer’s and frontotemporal dementia. Attempting to modify their existing design to target a new sequence didn’t work well, so they started the process over from the start and managed to find something that could cut the intended target in cells. For the researchers, this suggests that we might ultimately be able to influence the course of some genetic diseases by targeting the malformed proteins that cause them.
What do the results tell us?
The potential therapeutic use of this is complicated. Proteins are often difficult to deliver to the site where they’re needed, and can often trigger an immune response. Things get even more challenging if the protease target is inside a cell rather than on the exterior. That would likely require the target cells to make the protease, which would involve delivering the gene encoding it to the cells where it’s needed. So, there are considerable hurdles that would need to be cleared before we could potentially start developing therapies using this technology.
The researchers also highlight how the work shows some limitations of the tools. As used, they successfully designed proteins that matched all the physical constraints they were given: They folded up into structures that brought the amino acids needed to catalyze a reaction into roughly the right location, and latched on to specific target amino acid sequences.
But we don’t, at the moment, have the ability to tell these tools we want any specific catalytic activity. So many designs lacked some of the subtle details that make evolved enzymes such great catalysts. In other words, the tools are great at structure, but they’re not necessarily great at activity. And, while structure is essential for function, it isn’t everything. As the researchers saw, introducing random mutation could still make subtle structural tweaks that produced enzymes that were considerably more active.
Of course, this protein design software is only a few years old, and both developers and users might have ideas for incorporating constraints beyond physical location.

title: Recording device hidden in toilet paper found in top-secret OpenAI meeting room - Ars Technica
text:
It took OpenAI two days to notice that a recording device was hidden in a restricted executive conference room where leadership met to discuss highly confidential information, including technical progress, government engagements, and commercial partnerships.
Only those with special clearance are supposed to access that room. But the FBI believes the recording device was planted by Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer from Saudi Arabia, who became a permanent US legal resident in 2020. In a press release Tuesday announcing his arrest, the FBI alleged that chatbot logs and CCTV footage suggested that Alfozan—who worked as an OpenAI engineer for more than a year—sought to use the device to spy on OpenAI and risked leaking trade secrets in a way that threatened national security.
To conceal the USB device, Alfozan allegedly wrapped it in toilet paper, then plugged it into the back of a conference room television. The device was likely planted on September 28, and OpenAI found it on September 30 and quickly determined that its contents were encrypted, the FBI said. Days later, on October 5, OpenAI installed a camera in that conference room, and the CCTV footage allegedly showed Alfozan attempting to retrieve the recording device that same day.
CCTV screenshot.
via Liang affidavit
CCTV screenshot.
via Liang affidavit
Toilet paper-wrapped recording device.
via Liang affidavit
Toilet paper-wrapped recording device.
via Liang affidavit
CCTV screenshot.
via Liang affidavit
Toilet paper-wrapped recording device.
via Liang affidavit
If convicted of violating laws against unlawful recordings, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, the FBI said.
OpenAI did not immediately move to eject Alfozan as a suspected spy. Instead, it gradually cut off his access to systems while working with the FBI to analyze the recording device’s contents. Once enough evidence was gathered, OpenAI timed Alfozan’s firing on Friday with the FBI’s arrest.
Citing a Trump memo ordering coordinated efforts to maintain America’s AI advantage, FBI Director Kash Patel celebrated Alfozan’s arrest and vowed to continue policing efforts to spy on frontier labs like OpenAI.
It’s “essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” Patel said.
Catching an accused AI spy
OpenAI hired Alfozan in July 2025, but the record suggests that he started acting suspiciously in the past few months.
In August, Alfozan allegedly used an OpenAI productivity agent to figure out where and when sensitive meetings were held, a recently unsealed affidavit submitted by FBI special agent Lydia Liang said.
Credit:
via Liang’s affidavit
Credit:
via Liang's affidavit
Liang is a data analyst who joined the FBI after working for various tech companies. She analyzed the recording device that OpenAI found, which she said was a Chinese-made Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense.
According to Liang, the Seeed device “had been customized to obfuscate anything stored on the device, such as potentially intercepted audio communications.” And the microSD card had “a layout consistent with a potentially encrypted file system.”
In addition to reviewing Alfozan’s queries to OpenAI’s productivity agent, the FBI also reviewed an AI chatbot account associated with his spouse. Those logs showed user prompts referencing the Seeed device’s unique MAC address, the FBI said, while researching how to continuously record on that device, set up speech-triggered recording, and encrypt an SD card, among other queries.
Alfozan’s spouse’s logs.
Credit:
via Liang’s affidavit
Alfozan’s spouse’s logs.
Credit:
via Liang's affidavit
“These written prompts attributable to Alfozan and/or his spouse, indicate that Alfozan inserted Recording Device 1 into the television in Conference Room 1 and was interested in building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing, among other things, a surreptitious audio listening and recording device,” Liang said.
Second recording device found
CCTV footage allegedly caught Alfozan lurking outside the executive conference room on 10 different days in September alone, Liang noted.
Even more troubling to the FBI and OpenAI, it seemed that Alfozan had either deemed his plot successful and planned to plant another device or had noticed the camera stopped working and attempted to swap it out.
On the day he was seen checking behind the conference room TV, Alfozan also reported to OpenAI’s lost and found that he lost a bag. That bag had been left unattended in a printer room, the FBI said, where security personnel found it and discovered another Seeed device inside.
Alfozan seemingly did not suspect he had been caught, as he returned to the lost and found the next day and complained about missing items from the bag. When listing what had been taken, though, he did not mention the second recording device.
It remains unclear who the secret recordings were intended for, but that information may soon come out, as officials seem inclined to make an example of Alfozan at a time when maintaining AI dominance is a top Trump administration priority.
US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian said he would keep an eye on emerging threats in Silicon Valley.
“The Bay Area and Silicon Valley lead the world in developing tomorrow’s technology, and our Office will continue to stand at the forefront of protecting that American innovation,” Missakian said. “For us, it is a matter of national security. This arrest highlights our relentless efforts in partnership with the FBI to identify and prosecute those who seek to steal our technology, as alleged in the complaint.”

title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices - Ars Technica
text:
AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown.
By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms.
Challenging to shut down
Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.”
Smaller AI models require much less powerful hardware to run than do frontier models. Anthropic ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other types of IoT hardware. Company researchers found that by using quantization to represent the models using fewer bits and splitting the workloads into “shards” running on each device, the models were able to establish inference, meaning that the model weights loaded and could generate output.
The lightweight Gemma4-26B-A4B model required just 15 boxes, each equipped with only 4GB of memory, to achieve inference. The Qwen3.5-9B was able to configure other LLMs to run on eight of nine hardware types. Unlike traditional malware, which must be written to run on specific hardware or software, the model was able to use its weights to make configurations on the fly that were specific to the devices it was tested against.
This finding was the starting point for further research that asked: Would it be possible for small models to create self-replicating infections that run themselves on IoT devices the way traditional IoT worms, like Mirai, install DDoS code and other payloads? Unlike Mirai, these AI worms could pose a much higher threat, since the models could tailor exploits and payloads dynamically, depending on the target. Once such an infection chain began, it might also be harder for defenders to stop it.
“Such an ‘AI worm’ could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware,” Anthropic said. “Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload.”
Anthropic called these autonomous worms small weight-based replicators. The models ran agents that had access to common exploitation tools, like reverse shells. The flow of the attacks was (1) finding targets, (2) gaining code execution, (3) establishing inference, and (4) propagating to new hosts. A key benefit over traditional worms is what Anthropic said is the agents’ ability to learn on the job. Each time an AI replicator fails to compromise a specific platform device, it can leave a list of prompts, code, and notes to future replicators so they don’t waste time reusing the same ineffective steps.
Credit:
Anthropic
Credit:
Anthropic
Anthropic said the dynamic inference setup is the least studied and likely most challenging stage in the replication cycle. It requires a long sequence of decisions based on the specific hardware and software of each target and involves selecting compatible inference software, installing dependencies, and debugging platform-specific bugs.
“These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from,” Anthropic said.
The experiment shows that small models are becoming increasingly capable at solving those problems autonomously. At the moment, however, none of the light-weight models tested are able to mount end-to-end replication, meaning discovering new devices, using an exploit to gain access to them, infecting them with a payload, configuring an inference server, and repeating the process. The process is also painfully slow; Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over the 15 Android TV boxes, performed at just 0.39 tokens per second. That translates to a full-inference setup time of 71 to 150 hours for an unoptimized Gemma4-26B-A4B and 29 to 51 hours for Qwen3.5-9B. (The researchers said that the large model GLM-5.2 appears to be able to do so reliably.)
The company said that 30B-parameter models can already complete many of the individual replication steps now, although they make mistakes when performing end-to-end replication. The company went on to say that if small models continue to improve at their current pace, they may be able to achieve the same limited results by the end of the year and that “small weight-based replicators may be possible soon after.”
The experiment leaves various important considerations unanswered. For one, the Android devices targeted by small models had an unauthenticated Android Debug Bridge exposed. This tool is used during development and debugging but should never be used in production settings, because it gives attackers access to the entire device stack. And for another, the replication wasn’t performed by the small models themselves, but rather with GLM-5.2 to orchestrate the process while the targets ran a smaller Llama model.
Ultimately, the experiment demonstrates that small agentic models are becoming capable of setting up complex, distributed inference infrastructures across multiple machines. What remains to be established, however, is whether these models would initiate self-replication on their own.
“Despite the well-designed experimental setup, the study does not, on its own, establish that small models would autonomously choose to replicate,” AI researcher Xiaohan Fu said in an interview. “Providing reproducible agent setups, including the exact prompts and instructions given to the models, would help the research community better understand the findings and assess their implications. Such transparency is particularly important to avoid conflating the demonstrated capability to replicate with an emerging threat of autonomous self-replication.”

title: OpenAI says it will no longer train its AI models on the live internet, citing “significant risks” | TechCrunch
text:
On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access.
The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic, began limiting its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet. Researchers adopted these policies after months of incidents in which models pursuing training tasks broke into external systems in search of answers, collaborated on obscure message boards, and developed exotic hacking strategies.
“Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post.
OpenAI said that as recently as September 20, one of its frontier models exploited a misconfiguration to access the internet. That led the company to pause training work for the rest of the month so it could develop and test new approaches to securing its models.
The decision to train these models in sandboxes cut off from the internet is notable because employees at frontier labs have insisted that doing so would be nearly infeasible.
Keeping AI data centers separate from the internet “would need research teams to essentially be embedded inside of data centers in Iowa or wherever else around the world,” former OpenAI researcher Steven Adler told Fortune this month. “It’s a lot of overhead, and it isn’t clear to me that the safety benefits of it are large enough to merit just how large a tax it would be for a company to do it unilaterally.”
“In nearly every post I make on X, without fail, I get between five and ten comments about my inability to secure a sandbox, or asking why the hell we can’t just unplug the model from the internet,” an anonymous security engineer at OpenAI wrote in a September post on X. “These comments reflect a widening gap between where a lot of organizations and people are today and what the frontier labs are dealing with. There is also a general misunderstanding of how model training and evaluation work at these labs.”
The engineer, whose role has been confirmed previously by OpenAI, described how complex the training runs launched by OpenAI engineers are, noting that they require access a variety of resources and tools across many domains, and that thousands of researchers build, modify and test the environments. “So is it as easy as just putting it in a sandbox? No, it’s not,” he concluded.
Now, OpenAI says that “we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet.” That comes after the company deployed swarms of agents in red-teaming exercises that attempted to escape from their sandbox. That effort revealed a range of vulnerabilities that convinced the lab to adopt its new approach.
To meet that requirement while still reaching its training goals, the lab said it created a “a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems.”
Whether that strategy will perform as well as letting models run freely on the open internet remains to be seen, but it is noteworthy that both frontier labs have determined their most powerful technology can’t be left unsupervised on the digital commons.

title: OpenAI, Google pushing new AI models easily tricked into making nudes, researchers say - Ars Technica
text:
Safety researchers continue to warn that a large volume of AI-generated explicit content is spreading unchecked, while regulators do little to meaningfully stop it.
This non-consensual content is commonly shared in text and direct messages or stored in private clouds where it’s less likely to be detected or reported, a Google co-authored study of Internet users across the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom found this July. That’s why the “most critical intervention point” remains at the source: the harmful AI tools used to make the fake sexual images, Google researchers concluded.
Yet red-teaming in recent months suggests that as some of the leading AI image generators from Google and OpenAI become more capable, they may be getting worse at blocking explicit outputs.
Raising the red flag are researchers at White Circle, a public benefit corporation backed by senior leaders and researchers from Anthropic, DeepMind, Hugging Face, and OpenAI. It was founded after CEO Denis Shilov posted one of the most famous universal jailbreaks of leading models in October 2024. Bent on breaking models to conduct thorough safety testing, White Circle helps companies detect and deter threats when implementing advanced AI systems that may not always behave as expected.
Testing how well text-to-image models block banned content categories is a key research direction for White Circle, and Shilov thinks their latest findings are “horrifying” enough to share with the public.
Simple to bypass
In a little-noticed preprint published last month, White Circle researchers exposed flaws in the guardrails of DALL·E 3, Google’s Nano Banana 2, and GPT-Image-2. In a press release, they explained that “using just off-the-shelf tools, available online for anyone to download, and by sending API calls, White Circle was able to use the novel attack method to bypass the safety filters.” In the best case, on DALL·E 3, about 13 percent of the attack prompts produced images that human reviewers confirmed as explicit. The rate was under 10 percent for Nano Banana 2 and about 3 percent for GPT-Image-2.
“Critically, none of these requests required custom-built or frontier AI models,” White Circle warned.
Researchers reviewed the outputs to verify the bypass rate, which White Circle noted is “the highest of any method tested under the same standard.” The key takeaway, they suggested, is that, “at a time when AI safety has never been under more scrutiny, the defenses leading labs have built are far weaker than they acknowledge.”
By publishing research like this, White Circle is positioning itself as an external evaluator of frontier labs, and it plans to open-source the entire attack pipeline so model makers can understand the true scale of the vulnerability and build stronger protections. Although the company has not widely promoted the research yet, it will share it at a prominent AI conference this November, NeurIPS 2026, which may increase scrutiny on Google and OpenAI later this fall.
White Circle has shared its findings with some frontier AI labs through “mutual contacts,” Shilov told Ars, but neither Google nor OpenAI responded to Ars’ request to comment directly on vulnerabilities found in their models.
Meanwhile, OpenAI and Google have released new models—ChatGPT Images 2.5 and Nano Banana 2.1—and White Circle told Ars that prompt safety testing using the same method showed “both are significantly more breakable than their previous versions.”
Neither company responded after Ars shared these new findings.
White Circle’s attack method can break down frontier defenses in categories, like explicit content, that seem easy to spot, which doesn’t bode well for more serious defense systems currently being updated to block other unwanted AI behavior, like hacking, Shilov told Ars.
“White Circle’s working hypothesis for this is either the newer models are more sophisticated and capable of generating a wider range of content, or that safety has been deprioritized in favor of capability,” White Circle told Ars.
White Circle is also in early talks with government officials about third-party safety testing, Shilov said, which he thinks should be required. Mandatory independent audits could push companies to prioritize safety testing, which analysts have suggested largely takes a backseat as AI firms dump most of their resources into compute and AI infrastructure.
“They should be investing much more into safety measures and security measures around their models,” Shilov told Ars. “And for us, it seems that they’re not actually doing this.”
“RISE” attack method iterates jailbreaks
To expose jailbreaks that are “reusable and transferable”—working across different leading models—White Circle didn’t limit itself to testing one prompt at a time. Instead, researchers sought out “patterns which work across multiple prompts and scenarios” to detect reusable attack strategies that could work across leading models. (Researchers noted that Midjourney wasn’t tested because “it does not provide a public API suitable for controlled benchmarking.”)
The team has dubbed this novel attack method “Red-teaming via Iterative Strategy Evolution” (RISE). It relies on two components: an attacking model that generates jailbreaks and a judge model that verifies if the output is banned content.
The “entire pipeline is built on top of widely available models,” Shilov told Ars. The attacking model is a publicly available version of Qwen3-32B with its safety training stripped out, downloaded from Hugging Face, and the judge model is Gemini 2.5 Flash.
“You don’t need to have frontier models to break defenses of a frontier model, which is very interesting,” Shilov said.
A lot of time was invested in making sure that the judge model accurately flagged explicit content, Shilov said. White Circle research engineer Dmitrii Kharlapenko told Ars that when it comes to testing image generators, the whole field of red-teaming “is very poorly calibrated,” with “literally zero papers” setting up norms. For that reason, it’s an area that remains “completely plagued with reporting issues,” which is concerning to White Circle, as AI companies push to capture markets by releasing ever more eye-catching new models.
For White Circle, the research aimed to build more sophisticated models that could simulate attacks on other models, Shilov explained. That way, they could “help defenders identify and address vulnerabilities before they are exploited maliciously,” the preprint said.
In his ideal world, Shilov thinks AI firms shouldn’t just face mandatory external safety testing but also third-party monitoring, much like the system used to prevent nuclear threats.
Then, entities like White Circle could possibly form a coalition to help detect AI threats in real time, without suffering from biases. Shilov noted that an emerging problem in the AI ecosystem is that basically anyone doing interesting safety work is likely to be contracted by frontier labs, potentially compromising their work.
White Circle has partnered with frontier labs. It previously took part in Anthropic’s bug bounty program, but ultimately found that program was “very constrained in its purpose.”
“The program is focused on universal jailbreaks on domains they care most about, defined by their own specific terms,” White Circle told Ars.
Research like their most recent RISE paper “certainly” wouldn’t have been covered by that program, White Circle said. And conducting that work within Anthropic risked constraining White Circle from sharing it with the public.
Anthropic has proposed going one step further and embedding third-party AI safety evaluators in its labs, which White Circle said would allow them to operate at a much higher level than participating in the bug bounty program. However, the public may not always be able to closely follow that work. On Tuesday, OpenAI and Anthropic urged that restrictive non-disclosure agreements should be required of external evaluators to prevent leaks of trade secrets, Reuters reported.
White Circle would not be willing to sign any restrictive NDAs that might prevent public sharing of critical findings, White Circle told Ars, so if Anthropic requires NDAs, that partnership likely would not happen.
AI nudes, CSAM increasing
Bad actors who are determined to make AI-generated nonconsensual intimate images (NCII) and child sex abuse materials (CSAM) don’t need frontier models and often use so-called nudifying apps designed for that harmful purpose. But Google’s research found that 20 percent of online users who admitted to making AI nudes did so “for fun” or “as a joke,” while nearly a third were merely “experimenting with tech.” It therefore matters how easy it is to break defenses of the most accessible models. Safeguards should be mandatory, Google’s research said, in order to shut down a “pathway into abuse” for “a subset of perpetrators who might otherwise be deterred by technical friction.”
“A burden of responsibility also falls on developers to implement robust, model-level guardrails, and provenance indicators to prevent the initial generation and subsequent distribution of synthetic sexual imagery,” Google’s research said.
Last week, the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) warned that urgent action was needed after expert analysts found “more photorealistic AI-generated child sexual abuse images in the first half of this year than in the whole of 2025, including imagery depicting children under two years old.” In total, 6,310 AI images meeting the legal definition of CSAM were found in the first six months of 2026, which is about 40 percent higher than last year’s total findings.
The UK-based nonprofit charity monitors CSAM globally and runs a hotline to support victims targeted. In the UK, they’re calling for regulators to introduce a safety framework that requires AI companies to prevent their technology from being used to generate CSAM, an IWF spokesperson told Ars.
Until then, IWF thinks it’s important for third parties like White Circle to “highlight where companies’ safeguards are failing.”
“Our analysts have seen how advances in AI enable the generation of abusive child sexual abuse imagery with minimal effort, removing the need for technical expertise and significantly lowering barriers to entry,” IWF’s spokesperson said. “AI tools can reproduce and amplify criminal content, accelerating the creation and spread of harmful material at scale. Any friction or step that can be introduced to make it harder to misuse these tools is a positive step forward.”
Just as outside input could help refine filters, IWF thinks that tech companies should also be working more closely with advocates to scrutinize models to better tackle AI-generated CSAM.
“Assessing CSAM is a highly specialized task that requires expert training and welfare support, and is not something for tech companies or machine learning scientists to take lightly,” IWF’s spokesperson said. “But safety must be baked into new technology by design—this includes testing models before they are released to market to make sure they cannot be used to create nude or sexual imagery of children.”
Possible mitigation
Using a method like RISE, White Circle thinks, could help frontier labs flag more jailbreaks more quickly and rapidly ramp up defenses to block harmful outputs. In addition to testing blocks on explicit images, firms could also use the method to prevent other banned outputs, like images depicting graphic violence or self-harm.
But the labs have not yet come calling for the reproduction pipeline, which will be shared on White Circle’s GitHub to help policymakers assess whether AI safety laws are needed to keep frontier labs in check.
Frontier labs won’t invest seriously in safety testing until it’s mandatory, Shilov told Ars. The preprint argues that existing automated red-teaming tools, which typically rewrite harmful prompts one at a time, are poorly suited to testing today’s hardened commercial models. RISE instead takes reusable natural-language attack strategies and uses them to generate many varied prompts, which White Circle says can help labs find and patch weaknesses faster.
“You don’t need frontier models or proprietary tech to break these systems; you just need a free download and the ability to make API calls,” Shilov said. “And yet the labs building these systems are the ones assessing their own safety, publishing their own results, and setting their own standards. This is further proof, if we needed it, that governments should be pushing for independent, third-party evaluation.”
Correction: This story has been updated to correct several errors. An earlier version described a passage from the RISE preprint as explaining how AI models could block harmful outputs; the passage instead describes the researchers’ attack method. It also said the method bypassed safety filters about 13 percent of the time; that was the highest human-verified rate, achieved on DALL·E 3, and rates for other models were lower. The story also misidentified the judge model, which was Gemini 2.5 Flash, and has been updated to note that the attacking model had its safety training removed.
Ashley Belanger
Senior Policy Reporter
Ashley Belanger
Senior Policy Reporter
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.
