title: Google Brings Gemini Personal Intelligence To Android Auto
text:
Google brings Gemini Personal Intelligence to Android Auto
In the coming months, the feature will also roll out to cars with Google built-in.
By Igor Bonifacic
Oct. 20, 2026 4:00 pm EST
Igor Bonifacic for Engadget
At the start of the year, Google debuted Personal Intelligence, a Gemini feature that allows the chatbot to pull information from your other Google apps to generate more personalized responses. An expansion in March brought Personal Intelligence to free accounts after it was previously only available to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. And now Google has begun rolling out the feature to Android Auto users.
In practice, the company says today's update will improve Gemini's reasoning capabilities in cars. It will also make the assistant capable of delivering more specific details as they relate to your questions and prompts. For example, if you're driving to the airport, Google suggests Gemini with Personal Intelligence will be able to answer questions like "what's my flight gate?" and "is my flight on time?" Provided you've linked your Gmail account, it can do all this without you needing to pull over to find a confirmation email.
More broadly, Google says Personal Intelligence makes it easier to interact with Gemini more naturally. For instance, if you need directions to your doctor's office, you can just say "take me to my doctor's appointment," instead of speaking a specific address. Recommendations are also improved. If you're in a new city, Google suggests you can ask for dinner spots along your driving route and Gemini will generate suggestions while factoring in preferences and restrictions, like if you're a vegetarian.
As before, enabling Personal Intelligence is optional, and you can turn it off at any point if you don't want Gemini pulling your data. You can also control what apps Gemini can access. Google is starting to roll out Personal Intelligence to Android Auto users globally starting today (with the exception of those living in Switzerland, the European Economic Area, UK and Nigeria). In the coming months, the company plans to bring the feature to cars with Google built-in too.

title: Chinese hackers spied on thousands of companies after breaching IT giant ConnectWise | TechCrunch
text:
In Brief
Posted:
9:47 AM PDT · October 22, 2026
Image Credits:Getty Images
Zack Whittaker
Chinese hackers spied on thousands of companies after breaching IT giant ConnectWise
The bad week for cybersecurity just got worse for thousands more companies, who were spied on by Chinese hackers following the breach of IT management and remote access giant ConnectWise.
Security researchers at Microsoft say the China state-aligned hackers broke into ConnectWise’s cloud backup service and stole application credentials that are used to establish data links between ConnectWise and its corporate customers, who rely on the cloud service to back up their company’s data.
By stealing the credentials, the hackers could log in to the customer’s Microsoft-hosted environment as if they were an authorized user and access their emails and other files.
According to Microsoft, the hackers used AI agents to rapidly hack into around 2,250 organizations at a rate of almost 3,000 attempted sign-ins per minute. Microsoft said this speed gives defenders “little time to detect and respond.”
The speed of the mass-hacks was attributed to the use of AI agents, specifically ARTEX, an open source AI framework that works with AI models to stress-test cyber defenses. The same AI software was used in a recent compromise of South Korea’s financial systems, many of which had weak security and lacked multi-factor authentication.
ConnectWise said it’s paused access to its cloud backup system and is investigating the breach. As of Thursday, the company said it was working on restoring the service.

title: Perplexity Makes It Easier To Run AI Workflows Entirely On Your Own Mac
text:
Perplexity makes it easier to run AI workflows entirely on your own Mac
You'll need a Mac with at least 36GB of RAM, however.
By Igor Bonifacic
Oct. 20, 2026 11:42 am EST
Perplexity
At the start of September, Perplexity introduced Hybrid Compute, an update to its Computer app that gave users the option to split their AI workloads across a combination of frontier and local models running on their own machine. In hindsight, it was probably only a matter of time before the company made it possible for people to run the platform entirely on their own device, because that's exactly what it's doing now.
Provided you own a recent Apple Silicon Mac with at least 36GB of RAM, now you can run the entire Computer experience, including the all-important harness and orchestrator, on your own machine. Like Hybrid Compute, Perplexity is pitching this feature as a boon to thrifty users and those who want to keep their data private. For example, with access to your Notes and Mail apps, you could ask Computer to generate a priority to-do list for you, without any of the data in your emails being sent to the cloud. "As more demanding workflows become practical to run locally, the machines people already own will take on a larger share of their AI work," the company explains. "This gives users more control over sensitive data and credit spend."
With today's release, you can choose one of two models to run Computer locally: Qwen 3.6 or PPLX Pro. The latter is a Perplexity offshoot of Qwen 3.6, which the company did its own post-training for to fine tune it for Computer use. If, at any point, you feel like the task you're running would benefit from a frontier system chipping in, you can authorize the software to call on one of more than 15 models. Any code or tool execution a task might require is done in an isolated sandbox environment. "These same security protocols persist in the cloud version of Perplexity Computer," says Perplexity.
Perplexity Pro, Max and Enterprise subscribers begin using Computer locally starting today. Once you download and install the latest version of the Perplexity Mac app, just follow the in-app instructions to download and install a local model on your machine.

title: OpenAI Says Its Models Can Help Banks Migrate From Old COBOL Programs
text:
OpenAI says its models can help banks migrate from old COBOL programs
The company’s models are now better at working with COBOL and other old languages.
By Mariella Moon
Oct. 20, 2026 8:01 am EST
Casimiro PT/Shutterstock
OpenAI's models are now better at building and migrating software in old programming languages with a dwindling number of programmers, including COBOL, Fortran and Visual Basic. As the company explains, 40 percent of world's banks still rely on COBOL systems, and migrating to ones that use newer languages would not only cost them millions to hundreds of millions, but also a lot of time. Programmers that work with COBOL are aging out of the workforce, however, so the banks that still use it will have to migrate within the next few years.
The company said its work on improving its models' COBOL capabilities is guided by developers and enterprise customers who submitted feedback. Coding models are apparently struggling when it comes to working with old languages. OpenAI created an AI evaluation suite called MultiLangBench, which asks models to create SQLite-compatible database engines in a specified programming language. It said GPT‑6 Astra had an average test pass rate of 87.4 percent across 20 languages, making it a lot of effective than GPT-5.6 Sol that had a 26.8 percent pass rate. COBOL remains the hardest language to crack, with Astra's pass rate being 72 percent.
OpenAI also evaluated its models' capabilities by having them migrate COBOL programs to ones that use C++, Java, Kotlin, Python or Rust, while also preserving what the programs do. For OpenAI's models to effectively help banking institutions migrate to modern languages, they must be able to preserve COBOL programs' behaviors, such as how it rounds numbers with excess decimal digits and how it handles missing records. In this case, GPT-6.1 Sol achieved the highest accuracy, which reached 97.9 percent, with high reasoning effort. At low reasoning effort, it achieved 86.6 percent accuracy.
In its post, OpenAI admits that a migration is only successful if "all tests pass." Programs that handle banking tasks, after all, would need to be highly accurate. "Behavior-preserving capabilities like these are useful for teams maintaining and modernizing older systems, though applying it to production software still requires expert review and testing against the system's business rules and dependencies," it wrote.

title: Uber puts all 30,000 employees on ChatGPT Work | TechCrunch
text:
Uber and OpenAI announced an expansion of their partnership on Thursday, with the ride-share giant telling TechCrunch that its entire global workforce — some 30,000 people — will now be using ChatGPT Work.
ChatGPT Work was introduced in July as an enterprise-focused AI agent that corporate teams could deploy for various workflows.
Uber originally piloted ChatGPT Work with 1,000 employees earlier this year but has now scaled up its usage to the entire company.
That earlier pilot was deployed to workers from across Uber’s various departments, including finance, operations, and product. Indeed, a majority of the early adopters — some 80% — were non-engineers, Sumanth Sukumar, Uber’s VP of engineering, told TechCrunch.
“They used it for a wide range of tasks: analyzing complex data from our operations to identify trends and develop recommendations; localizing training materials for different markets and languages; and building personalized interactive dashboards to manage their daily work,” he said.
Yet while the ride-share giant is now going all in on ChatGPT, it has not settled on exactly how employees will use it. “Our approach is to make powerful AI tools available across Uber while giving teams room to experiment,” Sukumar said. “For example, earlier this year we paired 30 AI engineers with teams across Uber and gave them two weeks to automate key parts of their job. Those ‘AI pods’ showed us how much opportunity there is when you combine technical expertise with a deep understanding of a particular job.”
Uber didn’t disclose how much it’s spending on the new rollout of the chatbot. Instead, Sukumar said the company will track how employees use the tool. “We’ll look at how employees are using the technology, the kinds of workflows they develop and how it helps them work more effectively. We’ll evaluate those outcomes and use what we learn to guide how we deploy AI across the business,” he said. Uber says OpenAI worked closely with the company on integrating the chatbot.
OpenAI has moved quickly to scale up its enterprise business as it competes with its chief competitor, Anthropic. Once known largely as a consumer brand, the ChatGPT creator has swiftly gained a loyal following with business customers, while other AI companies have struggled to keep up.

title: Meta Tweaks Its New Terms Of Service After Backlash Against Scraping
text:
Meta tweaks its new terms of service after backlash against scraping
The changes have alarmed publishers and others with business accounts.
By Karissa Bell
Oct. 19, 2026 6:47 pm EST
Panida Wijitpanya/Getty Images
Meta has tweaked its terms of service for business accounts after a swift backlash against an update scheduled to take effect later this month. The company removed a reference to AI training from its commercial terms, but there are still questions about its ability to scrape the websites, including those of publishers, that have business accounts on the platform.
The social media company initially shared a planned update to its commercial terms last week. As flagged by Nieman Lab, the new language stated that Meta would have the right to use web scrapers and other automated tools "to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them)" associated with business accounts on the platform. "Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features," the terms said.
That language, which was going to take effect October 30, raised alarm among publishers and other businesses. The concern, as Nieman Lab explained, was that these terms would seem to give Meta the right to scrape the content of any website that also has a business account on Facebook or Instagram, a group that includes the vast majority of digital publishers.Then Meta quietly updated its commercial terms again. It removed the word "train" and added that scraping would be used "in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products."
Here's what that section now says in full [emphasis added]:
"You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users' use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products (including business, commercial and related products to help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content, provide users information about your products and services, and connect you with users who may be interested in your products and services) and maintain the integrity and security of Meta Company Products."
In a statement, Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said the company had "clarified" the language to reflect that the new terms apply "only to our ads and business products." He said the changes "were not about scraping news sites" and that the company wasn't changing how it uses web crawlers.
The crawling terms we consolidated only applies to our ads and business products, and we've now clarified that in the terms themselves. As we said, how Meta uses web crawlers isn't changing, nor is how content owners can use robots.txt to signal preferences. These updates don't... https://t.co/dy5ClnYjTy
— Andy Stone (@andymstone) October 17, 2026
But Stone's statement doesn't address the fact that the new terms are still "a substantial expansion of Meta's scraping permissions," as Nieman Lab reports in its latest piece on the changes. A number of legal experts told the publication that Meta is permitted to scrape news websites with seemingly few restrictions under the revised terms. Though Stone claims the changes "don't give us new rights to supersede" content owners' robots.txt preferences, robots.txt is not legally binding. And AI companies regularly evade robots.txt instructions.
It likely also doesn't help that Meta has had a tumultuous relationship with news publishers. The company stopped paying for news in 2022 and killed its dedicated news tab in 2024. More recently, the company has cut a handful of deals with outlets to provide news content for its AI chatbot.
Now, media groups are sounding the alarm about Meta's new terms. Danielle Coffey, CEO of the News/Media Alliance, said in a statement that the rules "are outrageous and probably illegal." Theo Bamber, the top executive of the UK's News Media Association, told Press Gazette it was a "shameless landgrab attempt" from the company.

title: Spotify's current AI bet is about being the music service that agents choose | TechCrunch
text:
Spotify had a strong third quarter, reaching 788 million monthly active users and generating nearly €5 billion (around $5.6 billion USD) in revenue. But the more interesting takeaway from its earnings call was how the company sees people listening to music in the future, and why the rise of AI agents could be good news for its business.
Co-CEO Gustav Söderström thinks the music streaming giant is particularly well-suited to this shift.
“Spotify is in one of the few categories that actually stands to thrive in the agentic age,” Söderström tells investors. “This is because agents excel at replacing and taking care of things people would rather not do. People love getting rid of chores. But entertainment is the opposite. Nobody asks an agent to ‘summarize a song’ for them.”
Instead of opening Spotify, searching for an artist, and building a playlist themselves, listeners could ask an AI assistant to do the work for them. They might want music for a run, a podcast about something they’ve been discussing with an AI, or an audiobook recap that picks up exactly where they left off.
Spotify wants to be the service those agents turn to, letting people discover music and interact with Spotify through conversations rather than just its own app. Notably, Spotify was the first music service to integrate with Meta’s Muse assistant, and it also integrates with ChatGPT and Claude.
“Our goal is to be the media service that you use from any agent, really turning the growth of agents into a tailwind rather than a headwind. That is exactly what we are seeing now. We are seeing really good adoption of Spotify inside these agents. While other companies are maybe trying to figure out what to do and many are leaning out, we are actually leaning in and participating in the growth instead of standing by the roadside and looking at it,” said Söderström.
The market is already showing signs of friction over how agents access third-party services. Amazon, for example, has blocked Meta’s Muse from shopping on its platform, illustrating how major players may restrict outside agents when questions arise around access, security, privacy, or commercial control.
Spotify’s pitch isn’t just that AI should just make entertainment easier to find. It should make the experience more personal, too.
Söderström describes Spotify today as “an intelligent media service encapsulated as an agent, whether you use it directly through our application or via another agent…Spotify is now an agent that you can not only click on in our app, but talk to, ask questions of, and instruct. We can do things today that no other media services can do,” he said.
“For example, you can ask Spotify to go through your listening history song by song back to 2008, picking your true favorites, beat-stretching them by speeding them up or down, and then sorting them by key and BPM. Then you can ask it to mix them together into the perfect running playlist at your exact cadence,” Söderström explained.
Spotify has years of listening history to draw on, including the artists people return to, the songs they skip, and the music they discover. That information can help it make recommendations that feel more personal than a generic playlist generated by an AI assistant that doesn’t know much about someone’s tastes.
However, Söderström also emphasized that Spotify isn’t sending its listener data to partners. Instead, the agent asks Spotify for something, and Spotify uses its own systems to reason about the request and choose what to play.

title: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software - Ars Technica
text:
Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code. But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code, meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output.
A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.”
Cut once, measure twice
To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish, which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026.
To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations.
If there’s one thing AI coding agents are good at, it’s churning out a lot of code.
Credit:
Chen and Stratton
If there’s one thing AI coding agents are good at, it’s churning out a lot of code.
Credit:
Chen and Stratton
In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction).
The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write.
In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms.
Pull requests need changes a lot more often in the “agentic coding” era.
Credit:
Chen and Stratton
Pull requests need changes a lot more often in the “agentic coding” era.
Credit:
Chen and Stratton
While AI could also theoretically help with this review process, the researchers found that, so far, that impact has been marginal. Although 80 percent of measured firms used some form of AI code review by March 2026, AI agents were only responsible for 23.3 percent of all review comments and 10.8 percent of all pull requests, suggesting humans were still responsible for the vast majority of this work.
AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff. And while 95 percent of firms in the study have implemented AI coding agents by this point, many are doubtlessly still going through a learning process regarding when and how to best deploy them. These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems.
For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort. It’s the kind of result that makes us wonder if the considerable time and expense to get AI coding agents working is really worth it for most companies.

title: Homeland Security Bans DeepSeek Use In Federal Civilian Agencies
text:
Homeland Security bans DeepSeek use in federal civilian agencies
The decision comes a couple of days after the release of the company’s latest AI model.
By Jackson Chen
Oct. 19, 2026 12:59 pm EST
Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
The Department of Homeland Security has issued a sweeping restriction to remove DeepSeek use across all federal civilian agencies and their IT systems. In a notice published with the Federal Register, DHS characterized the risks of DeepSeek use as potentially resulting in the "transfer of sensitive data" of US government employees and vendors to the Chinese government.
Following the order, civilian agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency or Federal Communications Commission would have to exclude any DeepSeek products from being used, while also removing any existing related products. DHS said in the notice that DeepSeek's models could "contain malware or other security vulnerabilities." The notice also disallows DeepSeek from participating in any federal government contracts.
DHS' order comes on the heels of DeepSeek releasing its latest model, V4.1-Flash-1017, which the company called "smarter, faster, more efficient." However, it's not the first time that the Chinese AI company has run into friction with the US government, especially at a time when its cheaper AI models start to rival the likes of ChatGPT or Gemini. Last year, two US Congressmembers proposed a bill that would ban DeepSeek's AI chatbot from government devices.

title: AI disqualification yields new Nikon Small World in Motion winner - Ars Technica
text:
Credit: Nguyen Nam Nhat.
Last month we covered the winner of Nikon’s Small World in Motion video: Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in China, whose video captured tiny cilia beating in the airways of a child with a rare respiratory disorder. But allegations surfaced about Xu’s use of AI while making the video. Nikon launched an investigation and concluded that Xu’s entry did not comply with competition rules. The new winner is Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam with a video of a tiny roundworm and a single-celled organism (above).
According to a BBC report, some researchers expressed concern that Xu’s video had structural abnormalities and that cell features appeared and disappeared in a way one would not see in actual cellular biology. Others spotted what looked like AI watermarks embedded within the source files. Xu said he used AI “to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images”; however, he denied that AI was used “to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion.”
Founded in 2011, the Nikon Small World in Motion competition is a spinoff of the company’s Small World Photomicrography Competition, which has been around since 1974. Both are meant “to showcase the beauty and complexity of things seen through the light microscope”—one through still photographs, the other through photovideography, taking advantage of all the technological advances that now allow users to make movies or time-lapse images through the microscope.
The other winners also moved up a notch with Xu’s disqualification. Benedikt Pleyer of Bavaria, Germany, placed second with a video of jellyfish larvae suspended in water droplets; Andrew Moore of Howard Hughes Medical Institute in the US placed third with a video of synchronized cell division in neighboring cells; Patrick Hickey of Hypha Research Ltd. in Edinburgh, Scotland, placed fourth with a video of the dynamics of mitochondria and chloroplasts in Turtle Vine leaf cells; and Igor Adameyko placed fifth with a video of a tiny, colorful sea slug (Cyerce kikutarobabai) on the move.
Here is Nikon’s full statement:
After thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel, Nikon has determined that the winning video did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI. Nikon has adjusted the competition rankings on our website to reflect this decision.
This decision is based solely on the submitted video’s eligibility under the rules outlined for this competition. It should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent.
Advances in imaging and artificial intelligence continue to evolve rapidly, creating new challenges for organizations across many fields. This event has shown the need for Nikon Small World and Nikon Small World in Motion to revisit rules and evaluation procedures for future competition entries.
The Nikon Small World and Nikon Small World in Motion competitions celebrate excellence in imaging, both scientific and artistic in nature. We value the integrity of each image and video selected to appear in our winning galleries, and remain committed to upholding the standards of excellence that have defined this competition.

title: Google Gemini 4 Agents Just Beat Minecraft With No Human Intervention
text:
Google Gemini 4 agents just beat Minecraft with no human intervention
Agents split up tasks, warned about threats and even recovered items from dead teammates.
By Steve Dent
Oct. 19, 2026 5:19 am EST
Google
Google's Deepmind "AlphaGo" AI is famous for winning at Go, but the company's latest Gemini AI just mastered a far more complex game. Four Gemini 4 Argon agents beat Minecraft's final "Ender Dragon" foe with no human intervention by working individually while sharing tips, threats and mistakes, Google researchers revealed in a new paper. The experiment shows how general agentic AI models can now beat complex games, a feat that used to required custom AI software.
To tackle Minecraft, the Gemini 4 team set four AI agents into a sandboxed, randomized Minecraft survival world with a goal to defeat the Ender Dragon. No roles, strategies or game-specific tools were assigned. Each agent controlled a player using the open-source Mineflayer library and coordinated with teammates through in-game chat and shared memory.
During gameplay, agents quickly elected to split up tasks. They warned each about threats, gave lessons and tips, provided coordinates and even recovered items from dead teammates. Each settled into roles: for example, "janesick" made tools, "gyldenia" gathered food and supplies, "auratian" lit a key portal and "bulicame" built Enderman shelters and landed the final blow.
All told, the process took 27.23 hours, with the majority of time spent on the Ender Dragon. "The four agents wrote and ran 2,783 programs, exchanged 229 messages and died 605 times along the way," the team said. A fifth agent called "the Observer" monitored the session as an independent witness, both to check for cheating and to publish live and summary reports. The agents used 1.35 billion input tokens and the final cost was $810 at Gemini's list price or $1,620 at the standard price.
"To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents, achieved using only the standard Mineflayer library without pre-scouted seeds or other game-specific tools written by humans," the team wrote. "Winning required the agents to keep a coherent plan across thousands of dependent steps for more than a day."

title: Claude Duet app is Anthropic's bet on agents | TechCrunch
text:
The AI world is flooded with personal and productivity-based assistants, with new ones launching every week. Now, Anthropic is entering this battle in the hopes of gaining user attention with a new app called Claude Duet, aimed at rivaling Meta Muse, OpenAI Dots, Hark, Instinct, Grok Bot, and Fo.
Anthropic said the new agent is meant to cater to professionals and small businesses to help them with automating and managing tasks. The company is making a distinction from personal agents such as Instinct, by noting that Duet isn’t good at handling errands or booking tickets, and it can’t show you its browser use as it happens.
Instead, Duet can build a daily briefing for its users, create dashboards, or suggest actions based on the user’s data. Like other agents, Duet can complete tasks in the background through its own virtual machine while you handle other things, then come back to you if it needs your approval.
The launch arrives as the market shifts beyond AI assistants to agents that can work on users’ behalf. Many of Anthropic’s rivals are focusing on business use cases. While Meta’s Muse is a personal AI assistant, the company also released a version to cater to small businesses with connections to other apps. OpenAI’s Dots has a business slant as well, with its integration with professional tools.
Anthropic says Duet proactively delivers its recommendations as it monitors ongoing tasks. Built on the Claude Opus 5.5 model, Duet can connect to over 6,000 connectors and plug-ins in the Claude Marketplace. It can also make online purchases on users’ behalf via Stripe’s ⁠Link digital wallet or Shopify’s Shop Pay.
The company said sensitive steps like payments would require user approval. However, Duet won’t trade securities or move money between accounts.
Anthropic also released a new classifier to check each message to prevent sensitive information from leaking out. It said that, by default, the agent would turn down requests asking for credit card numbers and government identification.
Claude Duet is available as an app on iOS and Android, and on the web through Claude.ai for Pro and Max customers in research preview. Users have to join a waitlist to try it.

title: Nvidia's big bet on physical AI aims for safer robotaxis, humanoid robots - Ars Technica
text:
Investors bullish on AI data centers may be fueling Nvidia’s multitrillion-dollar market capitalization, but the AI chipmaker has also bet billions of dollars on physical AI technologies such as robotics and self-driving cars. Part of that gambit has involved developing a full-stack safety system that companies can build upon to reduce the risk of their machines harming nearby people.
Nvidia’s Halos system launched in 2025 with hardware and software tools to help developers implement guardrails in self-driving cars and other autonomous vehicles. Then the company expanded its safety architecture to more physical AI technologies by announcing Nvidia Halos for Robotics in June 2026—with the goal of enabling safe deployments of autonomous mobile robots in warehouses, humanoid robots walking around inside a factory, or even surgical robots.
“Now the AI models are getting capable, the robot hardware is getting capable, and a thing we thought is going to be the next bottleneck is safety,” Amit Goel, head of robotics ecosystem and edge computing at Nvidia, told Ars. “So that’s why we launched our Halos for Robotics to unlock the capability of these systems.”
The expanded safety offering for robotics comes as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described the physical AI business as already driving nearly $10 billion in annual revenue for the company during an appearance on the All-In Podcast in March 2026. Huang began highlighting physical AI as Nvidia’s second-most important growth category in 2025.
The tech giant has also invested directly in multiple robotics companies, including the humanoid robotics startups Agility Robotics and Figure AI, along with companies developing robotics foundation models. Nvidia has even partnered with the Chinese humanoid robotics company Unitree to provide an “open humanoid robot reference design” for researchers.
Expanding safety from AVs to robots
So what does Nvidia’s full-stack safety system for robotics involve? It starts with hardware, such as the Nvidia IGX Thor computing module for robotics and industrial applications that has an independent processor dedicated to safety-related workloads. “In the context of physical AI, you need to have your functional system and your safety system all running on the same silicon,” Goel said.
On the software side, the Halos operating system was designed to enable constant monitoring of “every hardware block” and “every software library” to swiftly spot any failures, Goel explained. The system also isolates safety-critical computing workloads to avoid any potential interference.
The system also includes the Nvidia Holoscan Sensor Bridge that connects sensor data with safety-related computer processing in a way that can easily identify corrupted data. This can be embedded in individual hardware components, like a microcontroller or Field Programmable Gate Array.
Last but not least, the Halos package also includes Nvidia’s simulations for testing robots in virtual environments, and an inspection lab program that allows robotics companies and other partners to get quick feedback on any safety “artifacts” that arise during robotic development.
However, adapting Nvidia Halos from autonomous vehicles to robotics required accommodating many different definitions of safety. The definition of functional safety for autonomous driving generally remains the same across different automotive companies and countries, Goel explained. But a robotic vacuum cleaning a hallway will have very different safety considerations compared to a robotic forklift handling heavy payloads in a warehouse loading dock.
“We had to reimagine and do a lot of foundational work to build a platform that is programmable, that gives all the hooks to the developers to actually define custom safety functions, but at the same time not break the underlying infrastructure that we built,” Goel told Ars. “Because giving flexibility can come at the cost of losing some control over the stack.”
Custom safety functions are also necessary because robots may operate in complex, diverse environments.
“If you are a robot coming down an aisle at six miles per hour, your senses do not see what are the blind spots and what is coming around the corner,” Gold said. “What the robots do is almost come to a halt before the turn, because they really don’t know what’s happening in all these factories, warehouses and hospitals—they’re unstructured environments and things can come from anywhere.”
Real-world robot deployments
The US startup Agility Robotics was first to incorporate Nvidia Halos into its latest Digit 5 humanoid robot, which is designed to work safely near people without requiring isolated workstations or physical barriers. The Nvidia system helped Agility bring all the relevant safety sensors and hardware inside the robot, whereas previous Digit robot operations have also relied on external sensors placed around the robot’s work cell to ensure safety.
“Now the robot is literally unchained—the safety goes with the robot wherever it goes,” Goel told Ars. “Now they can operate everywhere in a factory or a warehouse without having to set up a brand new infrastructure every time they want to do a new task.”
The Massachusetts-based robotics company Boston Dynamics has also been an early partner in the Nvidia Halos safety accreditation program, with a focus on building a safety platform that encompasses their Spot robot dogs, wheeled Stretch robots with a large robotic arm, and Atlas humanoid robots that could start deploying in the automotive factories of parent company Hyundai by 2028.
Other companies working to incorporate Nvidia Halos include the German company KION Group that deploys self-driving forklifts and other autonomous mobile robots, along with the South Korean company LG that is developing its own humanoid robot based on Nvidia’s IAI foundation model for humanoid robots called Isaac GROOT.
It remains to be seen if humanoid robots can become autonomous, general-purpose robot workers capable of handling practically any human task. But the latest push by the United States, China, and Europe to deploy more robots extends well beyond humanoids—and is putting robots to the test in many new environments.
“Earlier robots were mostly confined in one station doing one thing,” Goel said. “But in the new age of robotics with a generalized body as well as generalized skills, it is essential that the robots can do multiple tasks in multiple environments—and the only way you can do that in production is if you improve safety.”
This story was updated on October 8, 2026 to provide additional context on Nvidia’s investments and partnerships involving robotics companies.

title: How To Use Google's SynthID AI Detection Website
text:
How to use Google's SynthID AI detection website
It's a simple way to check whether an image has been created or manipulated, with a few caveats.
By Robin Bea
Oct. 18, 2026 7:30 pm EST
Google
With the proliferation of generative AI tools pumping out images, videos and even songs in recent years, it's hard to spend time on the internet without wondering whether what you're seeing or hearing is real. Google, itself one of the largest purveyors of generative AI, is now making it easier to spot its output. With the new SynthID Detector, anyone can check an image, video, or audio file to see if it's been AI generated, with some major caveats.
Google introduced SynthID in 2023, which adds an imperceptible label to AI-generated content, but there was no way for regular users to actually check for one until now. In 2025, it launched a limited version of SynthID Detector for certain researchers and journalists, and now it's available for everyone. While that may be good news for anyone looking for a way to verify whether a piece of content was generated with AI, it's far from foolproof.
How SynthID Detector works
Since the launch of SynthID, Google's Gemini AI model has embedded a watermark in everything it creates. SynthID Detector works by scanning for that watermark and giving users a simple yes or no answer as to whether one was found. To use the newly available tool, you just need to go to SynthID.com, upload an image, video or audio file, and wait a few seconds for Google to return a result.
That's a big improvement over Google's previous process. Before now, users could ask Gemini itself if a piece of content was AI generated. But for anyone who doesn't trust generative AI, it's hard to take Gemini at its word, and it's an immediate no-go for people who are trying to avoid the technology altogether. SynthID Detector also allows users to scan for watermarks embedded in content created by Google's SynthID partners, which wasn't possible before. That means the new tool can tell whether media was made with AI models from OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao, in addition to Gemini. Apple also participates in SynthID, but support for the detector to identify its creations is still in the works.
How reliable is SynthID Detector?
Robert Way/Getty Images
Since SynthID Detector is simply checking for a watermark rather than analyzing media for patterns that indicate AI use, it should eliminate the chance of false positives. That simplicity introduces its own limitations, though. The most obvious one is that it can't detect media made with AI models that don't use SynthID, such as Meta's tools. SynthID Detector is also limited to telling users whether it finds a label in an uploaded file, without providing any information on what parts of it were AI-generated.
Google says its SynthID signatures persist even if AI generations are edited after being created. While there's no guarantee that an enterprising faker won't find a way around that eventually, the company does seem to be taking steps to avoid that. A Google spokesperson reportedly told Ars Technica that users are limited to around 10 checks per day in order to prevent them from using the detector's output to find a way to remove SynthID. Users also have to be logged in to either a Google, OpenAI, or Apple account to use SynthID Detector.
How does SynthID Detector compare to other AI detectors?
SynthID Detector isn't the only generative AI detector available, but despite its limitations, it's likely one of the most reliable. SynthID partner OpenAI runs its own detector tool, which can pick out AI-confirming metadata as well as SynthID watermarks. Meta embeds its own watermark, called Content Seal, into its AI creations and offers a web-based detector tool, though a 2026 report from Reuters found that it sometimes failed to accurately spot them. Companies like Anthropic and Microsoft have also begun watermarking AI media, but don't currently offer consumer tools to detect them.
The downside of all of these tools is that they're designed to detect a specific AI marker, and no reliable detector exists that can spot generative AI across the board. Many researchers have developed their own AI-spotting tools, but they're not available to the public. And when it comes to the general purpose AI detectors that are openly available, their results are unreliable and prone to flag human-created work as AI content.

title: Nirva raises $33M for a pendant that only listens to you | TechCrunch
text:
Ambient AI is having a moment. Amazon launched a new wrist-worn device with Bee; a former Plaud exec launched ambient apps through a startup called Ambi, which aims to also build its own hardware; and Apple launched Voice Intelligence features during its iPhone launch in September. Now, a company called Nirva is betting on a jewelry-like pendant and its ability to listen only to the wearer.
The startup today announced a new $25 million pre-Series A round, adding to the $8 million it raised earlier in the year from investors like Lightspeed and South Park Commons, bringing its total raise to $33 million.
Nirva was founded in 2025 by two former Meta Reality Labs employees, Wei Lyu and Jason Chen, along with Hanying Hu, who founded a fashion and jewelry brand.
The company’s first device is a pendant, which can also be worn as a bracelet. The device weighs only around eight grams, making it easy to wear all day. Its battery lasts up to three days on a single charge.
Longer term, Nirva aims to release more devices.
Image Credits:Nirva
In a call with TechCrunch, Nirva CEO Lyu said that the company wanted to build a wearable that blends in with fashion, but also provides value to users.
“This is a piece of jewelry that only focuses on listening to your own speech. We are not like a voice recorder or like a meeting note taker. One key difference between us, Taya, Vocci, or Sandbar Ring is that we’re always passively listening to your own speech. So it’s always on. It keeps modeling the user and modeling your mind,” Lyu said.
For ambient devices, privacy is a big question, as people might not like to be recorded all the time. Plus, devices like the Ray-Ban Meta have instilled fear in those who are around the person wearing the smart glasses that they are being recorded too.
Nirva gets around this problem by asking users to record snippets of their voice during onboarding and building its model based on that. During use, the device filters out conversations or data captured from the other people around the device. That means it’s only recording the wearer.
In addition, Nirva by default doesn’t keep any audio data or transcripts after processing the conversations.
Nirva is positioning itself as a personal insights company rather than a productivity startup. However, its app shows you reminders or action items and ways to act on them. Lyu said that through its app, the startup wants to help users show up for others in a better way in their lives.
“I think there’s no universal way to help everyone to solve their problems. We are building a tool to help people to improve their self-understanding, self-compassion, and self-awareness,” Lyu said.
Image Credits:Nirva
The companion app parses users’ speech and creates insights that it infers are related to the user’s personality, including patterns, the people who tend to be around them, the places they’ve been to, and other daily notes. Lyu emphasized that the app shows users insights around their emotions, communication style, and ways they can improve.
Lyu gave an example of an incident when she forgot to thank her mother for something, and the app later nudged her with a reminder about this.
The company also said that, before it discards the audio, it’s able to track the tone, pitch, volume, and speed, which are useful for deriving emotion-related understandings that are then surfaced in the app.
Nirva will start taking orders for its devices in November, with an aim to ship them to early users by the end of the year. The $249 device will be available in silver, brushed silver, black, and gold.
The startup has competition in the AI wearables area. There are companies like former Apple employees’ Taya, which is also building intelligent jewelry. Plus, startups like Friend and Bee are trying to be companion gadgets as well.

title: Microsoft event debuts new AI-friendly hardware and Windows changes
text:
In its first live event in two years, Microsoft today announced its newest Surface laptop, outlined a host of changes coming to Windows 11, and shared a vision of how local-AI and agentic workflows could reshape personal computing for those in the dev community as well as home enthusiasts.
Surface Laptop Ultra
Originally teased in May 2026, the new Surface Laptop Ultra will be Microsoft’s first offering to take advantage of the new Nvidia RTX Spark SoC (system on a chip). The device has a starting price of $2,599 and comes in various SoC and memory configurations, with either a 5120-core or 6144-core Blackwell GPU and up to 128GB of LPDDR5x unified memory. It will begin shipping on October 16 and is available for preorder now.
While the new Ultra is clearly focused on the developer crowd, graphical performance was highlighted during the presentation to show off just how capable the laptop can be. By leaning on unified memory allocation rather than the physical VRAM limits of a traditional GPU, the laptop can assign its resources to handle modern gaming tasks as well as local AI development and deployment. The new Gears of War: E-Day was shown running on the system, meaning that even without a traditional gaming GPU, AAA titles are on the table.
RTX Spark Dev Box
Joined on stage by Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, President of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri also unveiled the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box. This is a $5,999 anodized aluminum black box “designed to meet the needs of frontier developers.” The Spark Dev Box ships with a custom “developer-optimized” build of Windows 11 pre-configured for AI development and local AI use. With 128GB of unified memory and the onboard Nvidia RTX GPU, the box claims one petaflop (that’s 1,000 teraflops) of AI compute performance.
The fancy new RTX Spark Dev Box.
Credit:
Microsoft
The fancy new RTX Spark Dev Box.
Credit:
Microsoft
The RTX Spark Dev Box’s design is quite sleek. The unit physically resembles something like an Android TV box or game console more than it does a traditional PC. In fact, the vent pattern on the top of the unit is reminiscent of what you see looking down at the top of an Xbox Series X. According to Microsoft’s provided press materials, the venting on the RTX Spark Dev box has 1,000 chassis air vents as a nod to the 1,000 teraflops of AI performance.
Local agentic AI is coming to Windows
Outside of the hardware announcements, Microsoft outlined a host of changes headed for Windows 11 this fall. OS builds featured on the Surface Ultra and Spark Box will arrive with an updated Windows software suite to support local model testing out of the box.
More AI is coming to Windows soon.
Credit:
Microsoft
More AI is coming to Windows soon.
Credit:
Microsoft
Copilot overhaul
Microsoft’s baked-in Windows AI, Copilot, is getting a major overhaul. The new Copilot layout will see things divided into three tabs:
Home – A starting place where users can interact with LLM models
Code – The space where Microsoft claims that users with no previous coding experience will be able to prompt their way to developing widgets and Windows applications.
Autopilot – The tab for interacting with AI agents. This is where users will oversee their agentic bot tasks.
Copilot all the things.
Credit:
Microsoft
Copilot all the things.
Credit:
Microsoft
New Windows Search Experience
Coming to a Windows PC later this year, the new update will allow Windows users to execute system-level tasks directly from the search bar. Rather than opening up something like Control Panel to adjust display settings, the user will presumably be able to describe the action they want and have the system execute it directly from the taskbar tray.
More AI is coming to Windows Search, too.
Credit:
Microsoft
More AI is coming to Windows Search, too.
Credit:
Microsoft
Microsoft Execution Containers
For those who might still feel a little trepidation about turning over their entire digital lives and files to AI bots, Microsoft announced the availability of Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), a security framework designed to keep agent activities confined to a sandbox. Available to developers today, the framework allows system admins and organizations to monitor active agents working within their systems and to specifically set guardrails for each, ensuring control over exactly what each agent is able to access.
MXC acts as a policy layer that directs compute traffic to the appropriate isolation backend. Depending on the workload, MXC can shift to a process container, session container, WSL container, or even an experimental hardware-backed isolation called MicroVM.
Put your work inside a Microsoft Execution Container! Which is hopefully way less scary than it sounds.
Credit:
Microsoft
Put your work inside a Microsoft Execution Container! Which is hopefully way less scary than it sounds.
Credit:
Microsoft
The hybrid approach
Bringing all of this new agentic workflow together with traditional Windows is a concept that Microsoft calls “Hybrid Intelligence,” which is a move away from cloud-backed AI solutions and a move toward local ones. Hybrid Intelligence will allow Surface Laptop Ultra or RTX Spark Dev Box users to allocate memory as they see fit for any specific application, as well as offer native support for local frameworks like llama.cpp and models from the Deepseek and Nvidia Nemotron families.
AI everywhere!
Credit:
Microsoft
AI everywhere!
Credit:
Microsoft
We’ll see if it works soon enough
Microsoft is betting big on local AI with the changes announced today, but questions about security and user acceptance still remain, especially in light of their past missteps and other recent AI agent mishaps. The Surface Laptop Ultra hits shelves next week—keep an eye out for our review, and we’ll try to figure out whether it’s worth the $2,599 entry price and what this local AI capability buys you.

A former security investigator turned tech writer, he writes to help readers escape subscription traps and regain ownership of their digital lives. He lives in Chicagoland with his family and a goofball husky.

title: How To Create iPhone Shortcuts With Apple Intelligence (And Why You Should)
text:
How to create iPhone Shortcuts with Apple Intelligence (and why you should)
One of the few places where Apple Intelligence actually makes a difference.
By Adnan Ahmed
Oct. 17, 2026 9:00 am EST
Adnan Ahmed for Engadget
Shortcuts has been around since 2018 but has only recently been supercharged with AI. I'm not the biggest fan of Apple Intelligence, but its functionality in the Shortcuts app is one of the few instances where I think AI actually makes a meaningful difference to the user experience. You can already load up custom shortcuts created by other users, but Apple Intelligence now lets you create your own through natural language prompts.
If you're running iOS 27 and own an iPhone that supports Apple Intelligence, you can simply describe a shortcut and let AI do the heavy lifting for you. Launch the Shortcuts app on your iPhone. It should come preinstalled, but you can grab it from the App Store if you accidentally deleted it before. Tap on the big + icon at the bottom — this will bring up a text box where you can describe what you want the shortcut to do in plain English. Once your shortcut is assembled, tap on the play button to test it out.
How reliable is Apple Intelligence at creating shortcuts?
Adnan Ahmed for Engadget
There is a lot you can do with the Shortcuts app on the iPhone. Theoretically, everything the app allows you to automate, Apple Intelligence should be able to help you build. In practice, however, this doesn't always work and might require a bit of trial and error or manual adjustments to get the shortcut working exactly as intended. Fortunately, shortcuts created using Apple Intelligence can be edited as usual.
For instance, I described a shortcut that would switch my screen to grayscale whenever I launched Instagram and back to color when I quit the app. It did fine for the first half of the shortcut but failed to disable color filters when I exited Instagram. I went back and forth with Apple Intelligence but ended up creating two shortcuts instead.
I had fun testing the limits of the Shortcuts app and Apple Intelligence, and in my experience, the app rarely refuses to generate a shortcut altogether, even if this means putting together a solution that doesn't actually do what I asked it to.
On some occasions when I fed it an impossible prompt, the Shortcuts app acknowledged that the requested task isn't possible. Most of the time, though, it strings together actions that it thinks are good enough for the shortcut. For example, I prompted it to "turn my iPhone off when the battery goes below 20 percent," and instead it simply locked the screen. Close, but not what I was looking for.
What else can Apple Intelligence do in Shortcuts?
Adnan Ahmed for Engadget
Being able to create shortcuts using natural language is helpful, but it isn't the only improvement Apple has made to the Shortcuts app. You can also create a shortcut that leverages Apple Intelligence to generate text and make sense of data, for instance. When creating a shortcut manually, select Apple Intelligence to access the Use Model action that can send requests to an AI model, process them and generate a response. You can also use the generated response in subsequent actions within your shortcut.
You can pick between the Cloud, Cloud Pro and On-Device AI models to handle your requests. You can also choose ChatGPT to take advantage of OpenAI's models. Apple Intelligence models seem to handle text generation quite well. I described a shortcut that would fetch an article from a URL, summarize it and save it to the Notes app. You can make it so the shortcut appears as an action when you tap the Share button anywhere. To do this, launch the Shortcuts app, select your shortcut, tap on the i button and turn the Show in Share Sheet toggle on.
Once again, results can be hit or miss and depend on how well Apple Intelligence is able to understand your request and put together the necessary actions to make it work. A simple yet effective shortcut I created saved photos I took using my iPhone's telephoto camera into a separate album.
When it works, the Apple Intelligence integration within the Shortcuts app is a godsend. Just be sure to tap on Edit after generating a shortcut and double-check the actions it has put together before relying on it to do its job.

title: DeepSeek reportedly raises $15B days after US restrictions | TechCrunch
text:
In Brief
Posted:
6:11 AM PDT · October 22, 2026
Image Credits:GREG BAKER/AFP / Getty Images
Kate Park
DeepSeek reportedly raises $15B days after US restrictions
Just two days after the U.S. ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek’s AI technology from their systems over security concerns, the Chinese AI lab has raised about $15 billion, about 100 billion yuan, one of the biggest funding rounds in the country, Bloomberg reported.
Potential investors include Chinese battery maker CATL and Tencent, the company behind WeChat, among others, according to the report.
The reported funding follows DeepSeek’s investment round in June, when it raised more than $7 billion at a valuation of $50 billion. The company was also reportedly seeking an additional $1.5 billion at a valuation of around $71 billion in July, with plans for a potential IPO in China as early as next year.
The Hangzhou-based AI startup is ramping up spending on AI infrastructure and open models for domestic and international markets, even as it faces restrictions in the U.S., the report said. Its expansion could further intensify competition among domestic rivals.
The massive funding round is the latest sign of investors pouring billions into AI companies around the world, including those in China, to compete in the global AI race. Chinese company Kimi developer Moonshot AI secured $2 billion at a $20 billion valuation in May. Manus AI raised more than $500 million earlier this month. Meanwhile, Chinese companies Zhipu AI (Z.ai) and MiniMax, which both went public in Hong Kong in January, have market capitalizations of roughly $29 billion and $7.2 billion, respectively, as of today.
DeepSeek was founded in 2023 by Liang Wenfeng, who previously co-founded Chinese quantitative hedge fund High-Flyer, which helped finance DeepSeek’s early development. The AI startup gained global attention in early 2025 with its free-to-use, open-weight RI reasoning model, challenging the dominance of U.S. AI companies. Liang retains an estimated 81.6% stake in its Chinese operating entity following its earlier funding round, according to corporate ownership data analyzed by WireScreen.
DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a TechCrunch request for comment.

title: “Software is over”: Bold AI developer takes aim at Adobe with open source clones - Ars Technica
text:
For a while, those hoping to avoid the difficulty and expense of dealing with Adobe’s Creative Suite have been able to use several free and/or open source alternatives that replicate some or all of those capabilities. Now, one developer is using AI-powered reverse engineering to mimic the look, feel, and functionality of Adobe’s well-known software with what he hopes will soon be perfect fidelity.
Artcraft got its start last year as a “controllable AI for artists” that allows for precise post-generation editing of AI-crafted images and videos. Over the weekend, though, the brand debuted its pivot to a suite of seven open source apps recreating the user interface and tools found in Adobe’s Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro.
In announcing those new apps on Reddit earlier this week, software developer Brandon Thomas said he used Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 to create “clean-room replacements” for Adobe’s closed source software in Rust (with WebAssembly versions available for use in a browser). And while commenters on Hacker News and elsewhere have taken pains to point out the new software’s many current shortcomings, Thomas makes the grandiose promise that the current “super early alpha” state will soon lead to something just as functional as anything Adobe has ever put out.
“We’re going to reach 100% [feature] parity within a month,” Thomas stated on Reddit of his plans to quickly squash bugs and add features with the help of community reports. Days later, on Hacker News, he amended that position slightly to say that “99% parity will take a while, but I’m sure it’ll be measured in months and not years.”
Is software over?
Thomas, who says he has about a decade of experience working on large-scale Rust projects, wrote on Hacker News that he was inspired to create his own open source Adobe software alternatives after being “bit by the dark pattern ‘cancellation fee’ one too many times.” Development of the totally free options offered here under MIT/Apache licenses will be funded, Thomas wrote, by selling token-based access to the pre-existing Artcraft visual AI model and IDE, which is offered as an imagery-generation option inside the apps alongside third-party models. This revenue stream will help ensure these apps aren’t “going to be some orphaned small-team project,” Thomas wrote. “We have a team building popular software for filmmakers, so supporting this is fully funded.”
Filmcraft closely mimics the look and feel of Adobe Premiere.
Credit:
ArtCraft
Filmcraft closely mimics the look and feel of Adobe Premiere.
Credit:
ArtCraft
Thomas is the latest in a long line of coders using AI tools to speed up the long-standing but labor-intensive practice of reverse engineering (i.e., replicating the functionality of a piece of software without directly copying the code itself). While that practice has generally been found legally acceptable, the ArtCraft apps could still face legal trouble if their “trade dress” too closely mimics Adobe’s familiar appearance and interface.
After coding exclusively with AI tools since February, Thomas said he foresees a near future when everyday developers can re-create open source versions of popular paid software to “take back the internet and own tech forever.”
“Now you can just create 1:1 functional equivalents, clean room, that are highly performant and cross-platform. Nothing is stopping you,” Thomas wrote. “We’ll replace Google Search, we’ll build our own smartphones, we’ll build better infra. We’ll remove all the ads and de-enshittify the entire tech world.”
“Software is over,” he gloated in an earlier comment, claiming to have “one-shotted Photoshop. The whole thing.”

title: Apple Updates App Store Rules To Ensure It Doesn't Offer AI Nudify Apps
text:
Apple updates App Store rules to ensure it doesn't offer AI nudify apps
Developers are now required to filter nonconsensual intimate imagery.
By Mariella Moon
Oct. 17, 2026 8:35 am EST
Tada Images/Shutterstock
Apple has updated its moderation policy for the App Store to make sure people aren't using applications, including those that use AI tools, to "nudify" or turn normal images into sexually explicit content. The company has long prohibited pornographic materials in the App Store, and apps that were specifically made to generate sexually explicit imagery haven't been allowed for a long time. Now, Apple also wants developers to proactively police the use of their applications.
Developers with apps that host user-generated content are now required to filter nonconsensual intimate imagery, including those generated using AI tools. They must give users a way to report offensive content and block abusive accounts. They must also prevent users from being able to upload those kinds of images, and they must remove any that slip through their filters. If they fail to implement adequate safeguards of fail to remedy any violation after they had been notified, they risk being removed from the store.
In addition, it clarified its rules for apps that use bait-and-switch tactics on the company. If Apple finds that an app has misrepresented its purpose during review and that it actually has "nudification" capabilities, it will remove the app from the store and its creator from the Apple Developer Program.

title: Fraudster jailed for using 10K bots and AI songs to outstream Taylor Swift - Ars Technica
text:
After pleading guilty, a 54-year-old North Carolina man, Michael Smith, was sentenced to 18 months in prison for using artificial intelligence to generate songs for a scheme that stole millions from music streaming platforms.
In a press release Tuesday, the US Department of Justice said that Smith is the first American criminally charged with AI-assisted streaming fraud.
First charged in 2024, Smith successfully ran the scheme for seven years without detection.
Starting in 2017, Smith began using fake email accounts and “fraudulently obtained debit cards” to create “thousands of fraudulent accounts” on services including Amazon Music, Apple Music, Spotify, and YouTube Music, the DOJ said. He then employed software that pushed the bots to continuously stream songs that he claimed to own, which the DOJ said were AI-generated.
By his arrest in 2024, he had created “hundreds of thousands of AI-generated songs,” then dispersed billions of automated streams among them so that the bots could avoid raising any red flags by all targeting the same song at once. All together, the fake songs generated substantially more streams than some of the most popular artists today, however. According to the DOJ, in a glaring example from April 2023, Smith’s fake songs were fraudulently streamed 80.9 million times during that month, while Taylor Swift’s entire catalog only got 9.3 million streams during the same time period.
Smith’s streaming fraud didn’t just hurt platforms but genuine artists who share royalty pools on streaming services, the DOJ claimed. By cutting into that pool, Smith reduced royalties across the board. Therefore, on top of serving 18 months in prison, he must forfeit the $8,091,843.64 that he claimed through his AI scheme, the court ruled.
For Smith, the outcome likely feels outsized, as a letter from his lawyers prior to sentencing urged the court that the DOJ should not be punishing one man for the “ills of an industry.” Since this is the DOJ’s first prosecution of this kind, Smith’s legal team suggested officials were making an example of Smith, while knowing that he did not actually pocket $8 million.
Instead of jail time, Smith fought for a probation sentence, noting that he was “profoundly sorry.” He further explained that he’d been offered a job that paid $5,000 per month to do “audio production, mixing, mastering, and recording for a record label.” By requiring jail time, the DOJ would only serve to delay Smith’s ability to pay back the forfeiture, his lawyers suggested.
The DOJ disagreed, though, telling the court that Smith engaged in increasingly deceptive tactics to sustain his artificial streaming, lied to cops when confronted, and needed a stronger sentence for deterrence.
“For years, Smith orchestrated a sophisticated fraudulent scheme that stole millions of dollars in musical royalties from rights holders,” the DOJ said. “The Court should impose a sentence that adequately punishes the defendant for his fraud scheme and sends a message to others that streaming fraud will be met with significant punishment.”
